h.title: HotLoop: industrial gateway, historian and alarms for PLCs
h.desc: Connect PLCs over OPC UA, Modbus, EtherNet/IP, S7 and MQTT, keep the history, and raise ISA-18.2 alarms, on a Raspberry Pi or across every site.
h.ogAlt: HotLoop. Automation loops for the real world.

h.h1: Automation loops for the real world.
h.lede: HotLoop connects to your PLCs and devices, keeps the history, raises the alarms that matter, and moves a machine only when someone with the authority arms it. It runs on a Raspberry Pi next to one machine or across every site you operate, and it grows with you without a migration. Home and lab use is free, and businesses run it on EmberNet, starting with a free Pilot and moving to Starter or above for a production plant.
h.stat1: Native drivers for OPC UA, Modbus, EtherNet/IP, Siemens S7, MQTT and Sparkplug B, CODESYS and more, each listed with exactly what it was tested against.
h.stat2: Flow node types that run your existing Node-RED flows, with every difference documented.
h.stat3: The whole Flow container image. It starts in a fraction of a second and runs on a Raspberry Pi 5. The full benchmark and method are on the Flow page.
h.prodText: Running in production at Shepherd Boy Farms, DayGlo and Trane Technologies through EmberNet.
h.loopH2: Sense, decide, act, and around again.
h.loopLede: HotLoop runs the loop so your people can walk away from it. It reports a dead sensor as a dead sensor, checks every rule when you save it, and refuses any write that is out of range or wasn't armed.
h.senseP: Reads real equipment over the protocols it already speaks and records the quality of every reading. A failed read is marked bad, so a dead sensor never trips every low alarm on the unit.
h.decideP: ISA-18.2 alarms, the industrial alarm standard, keep the trip that cleared on its own on the list for the next shift. Rules are checked the moment you save them.
h.actP: Every write, from an operator, a rule or an AI agent, passes through one gate with one set of checks, and every refusal is logged. See the write gate.
h.senseD: HotLoop polls real equipment over the protocols it already speaks and keeps the quality of every reading with the number. A failed read is marked bad, so a dead sensor doesn't trip every low alarm on the unit or send the night shift to check a tank that's fine.
h.decideD: ISA-18.2 alarms, the industrial alarm standard, including the alarm that cleared on its own before anybody saw it. It stays on the list for the next shift. Rules are checked when you save them, so a typo is caught in the editor before it reaches a batch.
h.actD: Every write, from an operator, a rule or an AI agent, passes through one gate. A value out of range is refused rather than quietly changed, and every refusal is logged. See the write gate in action.
h.prodsH2: Eight products, from a Pi on a shelf to the whole plant.
h.intH2: Every driver shows exactly what it was tested against.
h.intLede: Each integration lists the systems it has run against, so your team knows what day one looks like before commissioning starts. Protocols HotLoop doesn't speak natively come in through the gateway your site already has.

Businesses run HotLoop on EmberNet, starting with a free Pilot for evaluation and pre-production, and Starter or above for a production plant, with no keys to enter and nothing locked behind a paywall. p.desc: Compare all eight HotLoop products for the plant floor, from a Raspberry Pi beside one machine to a gateway that runs the whole site.

p.lede: The first four share one codebase and one version, and every one of them speaks every protocol, MQTT included, so what you're really picking is how much of the plant the box has to run.
p.db.edge-relay: None. It holds readings until the uplink is back, and that is all
p.intro: What each product has, not whether it's finished. For that, open the product's page: every piece on it says whether it ships today or hasn't been built.
p.r5: MQTT discovery (Shelly, ESPHome, Tasmota, Zigbee2MQTT), read and forward only on the relay
p.r7: Historian targets in the plant's own database
p.r8: UniFi network driver, with commands off until armed (the screens and events need the UI)
p.r10: Dashboards, per role and per screen, with panel mode
p.r16: A web UI and a login
p.upP: Outgrowing the Pi should cost you an image pull, not a migration project. Every product runs the same data layout, so going from IoT to Edge to the Gateway is an image swap on the same database, with your devices, entities, rules, alarms, history, and users already there. Going back down deletes nothing: what the smaller product doesn't have just sits there until you come back. The move has been run on a plain Linux box, IoT to Edge to the Gateway on one database. On Kubernetes it is a chart upgrade, and a backup first is the habit that makes it boring.
p.keysP: No license keys, and nothing unlocks at runtime. The product is what got compiled, so a feature that isn't in your image can't be flipped on by accident, and nobody can flip one off to squeeze you later. All of HotLoop is free to use. Every product is under the HotLoop Source License Agreement 1.0, free for home and lab. What that means for you.

iot.title: HotLoop IoT: the automation base, built in Go for OT
iot.desc: HotLoop IoT is the automation base for the plant floor, written in Go, with MQTT discovery. {version} is out. Free for home and lab.
iot.ogAlt: HotLoop IoT, the automation base, built in Go for OT.
iot.h1: The automation base for the plant floor.
iot.lede: IoT is the automation base for the plant floor. One small program reads your equipment, keeps the history, raises the alarm, and moves a machine only after you arm that one tag. Start it on a Raspberry Pi today, and move it up to Edge or the Gateway later without losing your devices, tags or history. The rest of this page shows how.
iot.nTitle: HotLoop IoT {version} is out, and you can run it tonight.
iot.nBody: It ships beside the Gateway, Edge, and the Edge Relay, from the same release, every time. It runs on a PC, a server, or a Raspberry Pi, including the 32-bit ones, it is about 29 MB on a Pi, and it installs with no login and no license key. MQTT discovery is built in: IoT finds your Shelly, ESPHome, Tasmota, and Zigbee2MQTT gear by itself instead of making you type topics.
iot.h1b: Everything is an entity, and everything else is built on that.
iot.p1a: A tag is what a driver talks about: a register, a node address, a data block offset. An entity is what people talk about: the zone 1 temperature, the conveyor run switch. IoT puts every signal behind an entity whose identity never changes. Somebody deletes the tag and re-imports it during a PLC change? The entity comes back as the same thing, so the rule that watches the oven temperature keeps working instead of quietly dying.
iot.p1b: Every line is ours, written in Go, for OT. Nothing embedded, bridged, or forked, so when something breaks at 3am there's one codebase to read and nobody else's bug to wait on. Every command goes through the one write gate, and a failed read is bad quality, never a zero.
iot.h2b: Everything above IoT is IoT plus more.
iot.p2a: Edge is IoT plus the machine layer. The Gateway is everything in Edge plus fleet, multi-site, and reports. The Edge Relay is the headless one. One codebase, one release, four products, so a fix in IoT is a fix in all of them the same day.
iot.p2b: Its database is {db}, picked by a setting. SQLite for the Pi on the shelf with no second container, PostgreSQL when it grows up. IoT keeps 30 days of history by default, because Pi disks are small. Moving up to Edge or the Gateway keeps your data and your config, so starting small doesn't paint you into a corner.
iot.h2c: It senses, decides, shows, and tells, and it says how sure it is.
iot.pr1: It reads. Every protocol driver HotLoop has, plus MQTT with an embedded broker, and gear that announces itself on MQTT (ESPHome, Zigbee2MQTT, Tasmota, Shelly) shows up on its own as read-only, so a device announcing itself never earns the right to flip a relay. Every reading keeps its quality, and a dead sensor reads bad, never zero.
iot.pr2: It decides. Automations are checked when you save them, so a broken rule dies in the editor and not at 3am. ISA-18.2 alarms keep the trip that fixed itself on the list until somebody saw it. Scripts and recipes put the plant's routines in one named place, and every one runs through the same write gate.
iot.pr3: It shows. Dashboards fold from a panel PC down to a phone, can be bound to a physical screen, and command nothing themselves. The logbook puts state changes, writes, alarms and rule runs on one timeline, so "what happened right before?" is one list.
iot.pr4: It tells, and it lets an agent in carefully. ntfy, Gotify, Discord, webhooks and email, and an Acknowledge button on ntfy or the Discord bot really acknowledges. AI agents read the whole plant and touch only what you armed, never without a stated reason that lands in the log. The consequence: you can walk away from it.
iot.cdLabel: Every piece, and where each one stands
iot.statusNote: "{released}" means it ships in the published release, and you can run it tonight. "{building}" means somebody is writing it right now. "{planned}" means exactly that.
iot.h2d: On a cluster, or on a plain Linux box.
iot.lede2: Two ways in, and both start on boot, come back when they die, and update themselves safely. Kubernetes gets a chart. A Pi or a small PC outside any cluster gets a service that follows the stable release. Either way you can start small and move up a product later without losing your devices, tags or history.
iot.k8sP: The database is a setting: PostgreSQL by default, or SQLite, which means no database container at all and is what a Pi wants.
iot.hPi: On a Pi or a small PC
iot.piP1: Plain container service files that start at boot with nobody logged in. The install guide has them, and the Pi needs a current Raspberry Pi OS.
iot.piP2: The app follows the stable release, and an update that can't start is rolled back on its own. Put the database on a USB SSD and not the SD card, because history writes all day and SD cards die of exactly that.
iot.after: Open it in a browser once it's up, sign in, add a device. Then notice you can't write to anything. That's on purpose: every tag starts read-only and gets armed one at a time.
iot.h2e: Run on real hardware, so you don't find out at 2am.
iot.c1p: The service files that run IoT on a plain Linux box were tested on bare metal (2026-11-17).
iot.c2p: MQTT discovery finds real ESPHome, Zigbee2MQTT, Tasmota, and Shelly installs, and it was tested on bare metal (2026-11-17).
iot.c3p: The 32-bit ARM build is published and was tested on bare metal (2026-11-17).
iot.licP: IoT is under the HotLoop Source License Agreement 1.0, like everything else HotLoop makes. It is free to use and source-available, not OSI open source. Home and lab use is free. For business use, talk to us. No tiers and no license key.
edge.title: HotLoop Edge: store-and-forward and an OPC UA server
edge.desc: HotLoop Edge is IoT plus the machine layer: store-and-forward that survives a dead WAN, and an OPC UA server for your SCADA. {version} is out.
edge.ogAlt: HotLoop Edge, IoT plus the machine layer.
edge.h1: IoT, plus everything that lives next to a machine.
edge.lede: A machine's screen and logic should not depend on a network three buildings away. Edge is HotLoop on a box next to the machine: everything in IoT, plus an OPC UA server your SCADA can read and a queue that holds readings and replays them in order when the uplink comes back. When the WAN dies, the operator still has a screen, the alarm still raises, and the rule still runs. A cut fiber stays an IT ticket, and the line keeps running.
edge.nBody: It ships beside IoT, the Gateway, and the Edge Relay from the same release, every time. It runs on PCs, servers, and Raspberry Pis, including the 32-bit ones, it is about 34 MB on a Pi, and it installs with no login and no license key. If the box only has to poll and forward, the Edge Relay is the smaller one.
edge.h2a: A box at the machine that keeps working when the network doesn't.
edge.p1: The operator's screen runs against the box on the machine, not a server three buildings away. When the uplink drops, readings are held and replayed in order, flagged historical, when it comes back. Pull the power with the link up and you lose what was in memory, about one poll, and the docs say so. Your historian gets a filled-in gap instead of a hole.
edge.h2b: In the middle of the lineup, and not a dead end.
edge.p2: IoT is the base, and Edge is IoT plus the machine layer. The Gateway is Edge plus fleet, multi-site and reports, and the Edge Relay is the one with no screen. One codebase, one release. The database is a setting: {db}, with TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL built for time-series data) when the box keeps real history and SQLite on a small PC with a small disk. Moving up to the Gateway keeps your data and your config.
edge.h2c: What Edge adds, and where each piece stands.
edge.lede3: "{released}" means it ships in the published release. "{planned}" means exactly that. Everything in IoT comes along too.
edge.l4: HMI (operator screens), what is built and what is the plan
edge.lede4: HMI screens aren't a second front end bolted on the side. They're the dashboards IoT gets, bound to a physical screen, and that part is out in every product with a UI. The symbol library and faceplates below are still ahead. They use the same bindings and the same write gate, so there is one interface to learn and one set of permission checks.
edge.hBuilt: Built, and out in every product
edge.pBuilt: Dashboards, bound to a physical screen, and panel mode: the dashboard bound to a screen fills the panel, with no header, big touch targets, and it works with the uplink down.
edge.pPlan: The ISA-101 symbol library, motor and valve faceplates, and PIN sign-in for shared panels, so the audit names a person and not "panel 3". They build on the dashboards and the same write gate, and this page will say when they ship.
edge.cdLabel: The planned HMI work, in detail
edge.d1p: A fixed screen that scales and never shuffles things around, because an operator's thumb goes to where the pump was yesterday, and it had better still be there.
edge.d2p: Click a motor and get its popup: start, stop, reset, mode, speed, its interlocks, and its alarms, built from the motor entity that already exists.
edge.d3p: The ISA-101 standard for plant screens: gray backgrounds, color only for abnormal, alarm priority by shape as well as color. When the whole screen is gray, the one red thing gets seen. No 3D gradients on the tank.
edge.d4p: The dashboard bound to a screen fills the panel with no header, no tabs and big touch targets. It works against the box itself with the uplink down, so the alarm list on a panel is an alarms card on its dashboard.
edge.d5p: On your own computer you're already signed in. A shared panel signs operators in with a PIN or a badge and signs them out when idle, so the audit names a human, not "panel 3".
edge.lede5: One chart repository holds all four charts, and a box can move up to the Gateway later without losing a thing.
edge.k8sP: The chart runs TimescaleDB by default and keeps 90 days of history. PostgreSQL and SQLite are one setting away. Store-and-forward comes with the chart, and its queue is capped so a long outage can't fill the disk.
edge.plainP1: For a box outside any cluster, plain container service files start Edge at boot with nobody logged in. The install guide has them.
edge.plainP2: The app follows the stable release and rolls back an update that can't start.
edge.h2e: Run on real hardware, so you don't find out at commissioning.
edge.c1p: The service files that run Edge on a plain Linux box were tested on bare metal (2026-11-17).
edge.c2p: IoT to Edge to the Gateway on one database has been run on a plain Linux box, and each step kept the data and the config.
edge.nwTitle: S7comm and EtherNet/IP have run on bare metal (2026-11-17).
edge.nwBody: As with any new controller, confirm a value you already know at commissioning. Each driver's tests are on the integrations page.
edge.licP: Edge is under the HotLoop Source License Agreement 1.0, like the rest of the lineup. It is free to use and source-available, not OSI open source. Home and lab use is free. For business use, talk to us. Edge isn't a paid tier of anything, because there is no paid tier to be one of.
er.title: HotLoop Edge Relay: a Sparkplug B edge node
er.desc: HotLoop Edge Relay polls equipment and forwards it over Sparkplug B, with no database and no UI, and buffers to disk when the uplink is down.
er.ogAlt: HotLoop Edge Relay, a headless Sparkplug B edge node.
er.lede: You have a PLC in a cabinet three miles from anything with a screen, and you want its numbers upstream without putting a server in the cabinet. The Edge Relay is the answer: a headless box for a Pi or a small industrial PC that polls the equipment with the same drivers as the Gateway, forwards every reading over Sparkplug B (the MQTT standard for industrial data), and holds on to them when the uplink goes away. No database, no UI, no login, and no way to write to a machine. That's the feature: a box with nothing to click can't be clicked wrong.
er.nTitle: Edge Relay {version} is out, released together with the Gateway.
er.nBody: It runs on PCs, servers, and Raspberry Pis, including the 32-bit ones, it is about 15 MB, and it installs with no login and no license key. There is a chart for a cluster and a service file for a box that isn't in one.
er.h2a: It reads, forwards, and rides out a dead link.
er.p1a: It reads with every driver HotLoop has, forwards each reading as a Sparkplug B edge node, and when the link drops it holds the readings on disk and replays them in order, flagged historical, so the historian upstream gets the gap filled in. Devices and tags come from one file. A bad file is refused and the old one keeps running, and a file the Gateway pushes applies the moment it lands. It can even find ESPHome, Zigbee2MQTT, Tasmota and Shelly devices on a broker, read and forward only.
er.p1b: It has no write path at all. It can't take a write, serve a screen, or answer an AI agent, because every one of those needs a signed-in person to pin the action on, and it has no users.
er.h2b: Not a smaller Gateway with the options turned off.
er.p2: It is a different program, built so the database, the web UI, the automation engine, and AI agent access are not in it at all. A "relay mode" buried in the Gateway would be one setting away from a web server listening on a box nobody's watching. It sits beside IoT, Edge and the Gateway in the same release, and the Gateway's fleet management tracks every relay and can send it a restart or a new device file over the connection the relay dialed out on. Nobody drives out to the cabinet.
er.d1p: OPC UA, CODESYS, OPC UA PubSub, Modbus, MQTT and Sparkplug B, EtherNet/IP, S7comm, MTConnect, HTTP, SNMP, BACnet/IP, and UniFi. The same code the Gateway polls with, down to the reconnect behavior, so a bug fixed there is fixed here.
er.d2p: Births and deaths announced the way Sparkplug B says. When the link drops it holds readings on disk and replays them in order, flagged historical, when it's back. The historian upstream gets the gap filled instead of a hole.
er.d3p: Devices and tags come from one file, and a file the Gateway pushes applies the moment it lands: new devices connect, removed ones let go, changed ones reconnect, and the ones nobody touched keep their sessions. A bad file is refused and the old one keeps running. The connection upstream stays up the whole time, so the Gateway doesn't see a relay "die" because somebody edited a device.
er.d4p: It reads and forwards. It can't take a write, serve a screen or answer an AI agent, because every one of those needs a signed-in person to pin the action on, and it has no users at all.
er.d5p: The Gateway's fleet management (API only, no screen yet) tracks every relay you register, and sends a restart or a new device file over the connection the relay already dialed out on. The fleet list shows what version each relay runs, and an admin can approve an update a relay is holding. Commands need no way in to the edge box, and nobody drives out to it.
er.d6p: Run end to end against a real MQTT broker, polling HTTP endpoints, Modbus devices, and an OPC UA server, with live config reload proven the same way. Device discovery and the whole relay were also run on bare metal (2026-11-17).
er.lede2: Two supported ways, and both start on boot and come back when they die. A container started by hand from an SSH session is not one of them, because it dies the moment you close the laptop, and you'll find out from the historian a week later.
er.k8sP1: The broker and the Sparkplug group are required, and the chart refuses to install without them.
er.k8sP2: Your devices and tags go in the devices file. If a device carries a password, keep the whole file in a Kubernetes Secret, because plain values are readable by anyone in the namespace.
er.hPi: On a Pi or an industrial PC
er.piP1: For a box outside any cluster. A plain service file turns the container into a service: it starts on boot with nobody logged in, restarts when it dies, and logs to the system journal. It needs a current OS release, so an older Raspberry Pi OS is too old for it. It follows the stable release and rolls a bad update back.
er.piP2: The install guide has the service files, the device file, and the few lines to start it. Check its status page once and you're done. A broker that takes anonymous connections is a legitimate setup on an isolated OT network, not a mistake.
er.h2e: What was run, so you don't find out at commissioning.
er.lede3: It was run end to end against a real MQTT broker, Modbus devices, HTTP endpoints, and an OPC UA server, with live config reload proven the same way. It was also run on bare metal (2026-11-17).
er.licP: The Edge Relay is under the HotLoop Source License Agreement 1.0, like the rest of the lineup. It is free to use and source-available, not OSI open source. Home and lab use is free. For business use, talk to us.
gw.title: HotLoop Gateway: OPC UA, Modbus and MQTT gateway
gw.desc: An industrial automation gateway with twelve native protocols, ISA-18.2 alarms, a historian, and one write gate that nothing can route around.
gw.ogAlt: HotLoop Gateway, an industrial automation gateway.
gw.h1: Every reading is real. Every write is earned.
gw.lede: The Gateway runs a whole site from one box. It connects to your PLCs, drives and meters over the protocols they already speak, keeps every value with its quality, alarms to ISA-18.2, and rolls up every site onto one screen. A dead sensor shows as a dead sensor, and nothing moves a machine until someone with the authority arms it.
gw.nTitle: {version} is out. It is four products from one release, agents can write behind the same gate as the screen, a scaled tag takes the value you meant, and a CODESYS runtime is read by its own variable names.
gw.nBody: It installs on any Kubernetes with one chart, or on a plain Linux box, and both pull with no login. Already running an older version? Upgrading is a short read, and the docs carry the step by step.
gw.btnBreak: Try to break the write gate
gw.h2a: The top of the lineup. Everything, for the whole site.
gw.p1: HotLoop is one codebase shipped as four products, all in the same release. IoT is the automation base, Edge adds the machine layer, and the Gateway is both of those plus what a whole site needs: fleet management, multi-site roll-ups and scheduled reports. The Edge Relay is the one with no screen that polls and forwards.
gw.p2: All four are out in {version}. If you need one box running a whole site, this is the box. If the box sits next to one machine, Edge is smaller.
gw.h2b: Every write goes through one gate, and nothing routes around it.
gw.lede3: The screen, a rule, a script, an agent: same gate, same checks, same order. Policy lives in one place, so every path to a live press meets every check.
gw.after: An agent gets no side door. It hits the same gate an operator does, and it can't write without a stated reason. The audit row records who and what, and the reason lands in the system log right next to the write it explains. Six months later, every write still has its reason in the log.
gw.h2c: A failed read is not a value.
gw.lede4: Every reading carries good, uncertain or bad. A driver that can't read a point still reports, marked bad, because silence looks exactly like a value that hasn't changed. Alarms hold their state on a bad reading instead of evaluating it, so a dead instrument shows up as a dead instrument and not as a process upset.
gw.h2d: An assistant that can read everything and touch only what you armed.
gw.p5a: Over a hundred tools let an AI agent read the plant and, behind a switch, change its configuration, with the permission of whoever it signs in as and a required reason. An agent reads the plant in entities, the infeed pump rather than register 40001, and it can only act through the gate. So you can ask it why line 3 is slow and let it read everything, knowing it can only touch what you armed, and every write it makes comes with a reason in the log.
gw.p5b: It goes the other way too: a rule can call a tool on another agent server.
gw.p6a: Point one Gateway at the others and the Sites screen asks each of them the question it would answer itself. Each site keeps its own database, so a dead WAN link takes out a roll-up, never a plant.
gw.p6b: A site that doesn't answer shows as unreachable, with the reason, and stays out of the totals, so head office never reads a plant it can't reach as a quiet one.
gw.h2f: Twelve native drivers, each listed with what it was tested against.
gw.n1t: S7comm and EtherNet/IP have run on bare metal (2026-11-17).
gw.n1p: As with any new controller, confirm a value you already know at commissioning.
gw.n2t: SNMP and BACnet/IP have run on bare metal (2026-11-17).
gw.n2p: SNMP was read at every v3 security level, and BACnet/IP against an independent BACnet stack. Vendors differ about their MIBs, their object lists, and how they answer a request that is too big, so a new switch, UPS, or controller is still a commissioning job: compare the probe's values with the device's own display.
gw.h2g: The rest of the plant, in one program.
gw.lede8: No sidecar, no second service to keep alive, no runtime to babysit. One self-contained program that runs as a non-root user with every special privilege dropped, so there is nothing extra to patch and nothing extra to attack.
gw.c1p: TimescaleDB (a time-series database) when it's there, plain PostgreSQL partitioning when it isn't. Per-tag deadband, so a sensor twitching in its last bit doesn't write a row every scan until the disk fills.

tx.title: HotLoop Transmitter: OPC UA PubSub from the PLC
tx.desc: HotLoop Transmitter is a CODESYS library that publishes PLC values as OPC UA PubSub over UDP, written in Structured Text.
tx.descNR: HotLoop Transmitter is a CODESYS library that publishes PLC values as OPC UA PubSub over UDP, in Structured Text. Not released yet.
tx.ogAlt: HotLoop Transmitter, OPC UA PubSub from the PLC.
tx.h1: Put the process value on the wire from inside the PLC.
tx.lede: You want a PLC's values on the network as OPC UA PubSub, and the PLC has no PubSub library on it. Transmitter is a CODESYS library that fixes that: you add it to the project, call one function block once per cycle, and a UADP message goes out every publishing interval to a unicast address or a multicast group, the way Part 14 of the spec says. It needs no other library, no extra license, and no configurator. The consequence: a bare PLC can feed anything that subscribes to OPC UA PubSub, with a few lines of Structured Text.
tx.nTitle: There is no release yet, and no file to download.
tx.nBody: The library builds and runs on a real CODESYS runtime, and what it sends was read back by decoders that are not ours. It was also run on bare metal (2026-11-17). Nothing here is installable until a version is tagged, and this page says so until then.
tx.btnLineup: See the rest of the lineup
tx.h2a: Add the library, call one block.
tx.p1: Declare a publisher, add the variables you want out once at start, and call it every cycle. The block builds one message in a fixed buffer and sends it on a non-blocking socket, and the cost of a call is the cost of building one message, paid only on the cycles where one goes out. A bad address or a field list that does not fit becomes a state and a counter on the block, never a fault in your program, so the scan keeps scanning.
tx.p2: It sends BOOL through LREAL, STRING and TIME, and arrays, in two encodings. Variant is read by any subscriber without a layout. RawData is smaller and needs the receiver to know the layout.
tx.h2b: It lives inside the PLC, in the PLC's own language.
tx.p3: It has to run inside the PLC's own scan, as a library the programmer references from the project, so it is written in Structured Text, the language every CODESYS programmer already reads. Your controls engineer can open it and see exactly what it does.
tx.l3: Next to the rest of HotLoop
tx.h2c: It publishes. The other end is somebody else's.
tx.p4: Transmitter only publishes: the subscriber side is not part of it. It sits on its own release line beside the rest of the lineup. HotLoop's own subscriber reads it. It is under the same license as the rest of the lineup.
tx.h2d: One library file in the CODESYS library repository.
tx.p5: Download the library below and install it in the CODESYS IDE. This is version {version}.
tx.p5nr: There is no file to download today, so these are the steps for when there is.
tx.p6: You need a current CODESYS development system and a runtime that supports sockets and a real-time clock, which the CODESYS Control runtimes for Linux SL do.
tx.s1: Install {file} with Tools, Library Repository, Install, or install the .package with the CODESYS Installer.
tx.s2: Open the application's Library Manager, Add Library, and pick HotLoop Transmitter. Whatever it depends on comes along.
tx.s3: Declare an HLTX.FB_HLTX_Publisher, add your fields, and call it every cycle, as in the example above.
tx.s4: Download to the controller. The destination has to be reachable from its network, and for multicast the switches have to carry the group.
tx.note: The .compiled-library file is the same library without its source, for when you don't want the Structured Text visible in the Library Manager. The install page in the docs lists every error the block can report, and what to do about each.
tx.h2e: What was run, and what it showed.
tx.p7: The full runs are on the proof page, and the timing on the timing page.
tx.pr1v: The library compiled with no errors and no warnings in the CODESYS development system, and the example application built against it for a CODESYS Control for Linux SL device.
tx.pr2v: A real CODESYS Control for Linux runtime with a fast task, and on bare metal (2026-11-17). Two publishers, one in each encoding, seventeen fields each.
tx.pr3v: Every field equalled the PLC's own value, in both encodings, with no gap in the message sequence numbers.
tx.pr4k: Read by a stack that is not ours
tx.pr4v: An independent OPC UA stack read every value in the Variant encoding, strings and arrays included, and every numeric scalar in the compact RawData encoding. Compact RawData is limited by that reader for longer strings and arrays, not by Transmitter.
tx.pr5v: HotLoop's own subscriber read both publishers live and checked 21 values equal, including the string, the TIME, both arrays and two counters that moved between reads. It refused nothing, and every reading carried the publisher's timestamp as its time.
tx.pr6v: Every message carries the PLC clock's reading, never going backwards, and an independent stack read the timestamps of every message. The stamp is the PLC clock's reading, so a subscriber knows when a value was sampled, not when it arrived.
tx.pr7v: It installs through the CODESYS package tooling, the library appears in the System repository, and the example builds against it with no errors and no warnings.
tx.pr8v: With timestamps on, about 10 microseconds added to a 20 ms cycle on average. A cycle that sends takes 10 to 100 microseconds. If a stall in the operating system's send call matters to your control logic, publish from its own lower priority task. A small ARM controller can be slower than the machine these numbers came from, so measure it on the target with the block's own timing outputs.
tx.h2fnr: What is in the first version.
tx.b1h: One block, called once per cycle
tx.b1b: One function block sends one message per publishing interval, and it carries every field you added.
tx.b2b: BOOL, SINT, USINT, INT, UINT, DINT, UDINT, LINT, ULINT, REAL, LREAL, STRING and TIME, plus arrays of any of them but STRING.
tx.b3b: Variant, which any subscriber reads without a layout, and RawData, which is smaller and needs the receiver to know the layout.
tx.b4b: A dotted address, a port, and for multicast a TTL and the interface to send from. Publisher id, writer group, dataset writer and the interval are inputs of the block.
tx.b5b: Every message carries the PLC clock's reading, so a subscriber knows when a value was sampled and does not guess from when it arrived. Switch it off and the block sends the original message format. It needs the runtime's real-time clock component, which the CODESYS Control runtimes for Linux SL have.
tx.b6b: Messages sent, sends refused, publish slots skipped, the size of the last message, and the time the block spent in its last call and its longest.
tx.b7b: It is Structured Text, and every CODESYS runtime with sockets runs it. No other library, no configurator.
tx.w1b: The socket is non-blocking and the message is built in a fixed buffer. A socket error, a bad address, or a field list that does not fit becomes a state and a counter on the block, never a fault in your application.
tx.w2b: A message is sized to fit one Ethernet frame. A field list that does not fit puts the block in an error state and sends nothing, instead of cutting your data.
tx.w3b: This version sends in the clear. Message signing and encryption are not built, and the roadmap says so.
tx.w4b: It publishes. The subscriber side is not part of this library.
tx.pl1v: Sub-second timestamps, several DataSetMessages in one NetworkMessage, delta frames and keep-alives, WSTRING, and a per-field status.
tx.pl2v: Message security, chunked messages, the subscriber side, and an MQTT transport.
tx.h2i: Under the HotLoop Source License Agreement 1.0.
tx.p8: Like every HotLoop product. It is free to use and source-available, not OSI open source. Home and lab use is free. The license lets you build the library into your own PLC projects and deliver or sell the compiled result to your customers, never the library or its files themselves.
cs.title: HotLoop Cascade: workflows that survive a reboot
cs.desc: HotLoop Cascade turns an alarm, a webhook, a schedule, or MQTT into a checkpointed workflow that survives a reboot. {version} is out. Free for home and lab.
cs.ogAlt: HotLoop Cascade, durable workflows for the plant.
cs.h1: The plant talking to everything else, without losing the job.
cs.lede: An alarm trips at 2 a.m. and the maintenance ticket has to exist by morning, even though the network was down for ten minutes. Cascade is the engine that makes that true. An alarm, a webhook, a schedule, a new row, or a burst of MQTT becomes a batch of items, the items run through steps that call real systems with real credentials, and every step is checkpointed. Pull the plug halfway through and the job finishes when the box comes back.
cs.btnLineup: See the rest of the lineup
cs.h2a: A retry is a row in the database, so nothing is waiting on luck.
cs.p1: A step that fails is retried from where it stopped. A webhook that arrives while Cascade is down is in a durable inbox when it comes up. A schedule fires each slot exactly once, no matter how many copies of Cascade are looking. You build all of that by drawing a workflow, not by writing it, and a run is drawn the way it ran, step by step, so a failure is something you look at, not something you reconstruct from a log. What starts a workflow: a HotLoop alarm or tag reading, a webhook, a schedule, an MQTT burst, a file that shows up, or a new email in an IMAP mailbox.
cs.h2b: Real systems, with credentials that don't leak.
cs.p2: HTTP, PostgreSQL and the other databases, email, files, MQTT, and the notifiers: ntfy, Discord, and Gotify. HotLoop steps read tags and alarms, acknowledge an alarm, call a service, run a script, or apply a recipe, and every command crosses HotLoop's write gate with a reason in its audit trail. Credentials, OAuth2 included, sit in a vault sealed by a key outside the database. A workflow exported as JSON from another tool comes across with what Cascade is sure of, and the rest comes across switched off.
cs.h2c: Everything Cascade can do is a screen, on a box with no internet.
cs.lede3: The editor is built into the binary and fetches nothing from anywhere. Workflows live in projects and folders that nest as deep as the plant does: area, line, cell. These are real screenshots, of a demo plant with a week of real runs.
cs.s1AltD: Cascade workflows, in folders, in dark
cs.s1Cap: Workflows in folders. A person moves one from its own row.
cs.s2Alt: A failed run, drawn as it ran, with how every step did
cs.s2Cap: A failed run, drawn as it ran. Retry it from the step that failed, and the steps before it keep what they did, so a write that already happened doesn't happen twice.
cs.h2d: It signs in the way your plant already does.
cs.p4: Passwords with enforced MFA, passkeys, OIDC, SAML, and LDAP or Active Directory, with roles from groups. SCIM lets your identity provider make and switch off accounts without anyone touching a screen. Roles are yours to define. Credentials can live in OpenBao or HashiCorp Vault, so a password rotates where you already rotate it. The audit log and finished runs can stream to your log collector. A database blink never signs everyone out. An agent can sign in with an API key and do what that key's holder could do, reading and writing, with the reason for every change in the audit log.
cs.h2e: Podman with Quadlet, or k3s with Helm.
cs.p5: One file and a volume is Cascade on SQLite on a Raspberry Pi. On Postgres, it is a server, a worker, and the database, and Postgres is the queue too, so there is no extra queue service to patch. Both start at boot, restart on failure, and run locked down, non-root, with every special privilege dropped. On Kubernetes the chart can split it into parts that scale separately. Metrics come with it, and every execution is one trace with a step for each node, so a stuck job shows up on a graph. With no collector named, nothing is sent.
cs.h2f: Four refusals, and each one is on purpose.
cs.r1h: It won't write to your equipment.
cs.r1m: Anything that moves a valve or changes a setpoint goes through HotLoop's write gate, so the gate's audit sees every write no matter which workflow started it.
cs.r2h: It won't run JavaScript in your fields.
cs.r2p: Field expressions use HotLoop's small automation language, which can't touch the operating system, the network, or the files.
cs.r2m: JavaScript lives in one place, the Code step, locked in its own box with no network and no files.
cs.r3p: Single sign-on, enforced MFA, roles, audit, version history, scoped API keys, and high-availability workers are in for everyone. There is no license check anywhere.
cs.r4p: No license server and no cloud dependency. Telemetry is opt-in, off by default, and documented down to the field when it lands.
cs.h2g: Pull {version} with Podman, or install the chart with Helm.
cs.lede7: The image and the chart are public and pull with no login, on amd64 and arm64, so a Pi and a server both get the right one. The image is ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-cascade and the chart is hotloop-cascade in the same registry.
cs.podmanP: The Quadlet units follow :stable, and Podman's auto-update timer moves them to each release. An update that doesn't come up healthy is rolled back.
cs.k3sP: One pod on SQLite by default. Split into server and workers on PostgreSQL with --set split=true.
cs.note7: Take a backup before you turn updates on, because a rollback puts the old version back and does not undo a database change. Keep a copy of the key that seals stored credentials somewhere that isn't the box, because without it every stored credential is unreadable. Coming from the earliest releases? Read the 1.0.0 notes first. The full steps are in the docs.
cs.lede8: What is out is the engine, the identity and governance work, the editor, and the agent interface. The workflow file format and the API can still change. Every phase below is planned work, and none of it is a paid tier.
cs.ph1d: Git source control and environments, and protected instances. Rate limits, retention, backup and restore, and several Cascade servers on one database are already out.
cs.ph2d: A published connector spec, a plugin SDK, and forms with human approval steps that work from a phone.
cs.ph3d: LLM and agent steps, and a builder that uses your own model. None of it exists yet. Agents can already drive Cascade from outside, over MCP.
cs.note8: The details, in the order the work is in, are on the Cascade roadmap.
cs.licP: Cascade is under the HotLoop Source License Agreement 1.0, like every HotLoop product. It is free to use and source-available, not OSI open source. Home and lab use is free. For business use, talk to us.
ux.title: UniFi in HotLoop: read first, commands armed by you
ux.desc: A native UniFi integration for HotLoop, written in Go. The Network driver, screens, events and armed commands are out. Protect, Access, and PDUs come next.
ux.ogAlt: UniFi in HotLoop, with screens, events and armed commands.
ux.h1: Your UniFi network, next to the machines it feeds.
ux.lede: When a PLC goes quiet, the first question is always the same: is it the PLC or the wire? Today you answer it by walking to the UniFi app, or to the rack. HotLoop has a native UniFi integration, built in Go from scratch, so the answer sits on the same screen as the machine: which switch port it's on, whether that port is up, and what it's drawing.
ux.nTitle: The driver, the screens, the events, and the first commands are out.
ux.nBody: The Network driver, the clients and OT watch, the screens, and the events are out, and the Edge Relay can poll a console too. A command changes your network only after a person arms that tag, and it goes through the write gate like any other write, so nothing cycles a port or changes a setting until you say so. It lives in the base of the lineup, so every HotLoop product gets it. The setup is in the docs.
ux.h2a: A dead backup link reads dead.
ux.p1: The first time we pointed the driver at a real console, it said the 5G backup WAN was up. It wasn't. It had been unplugged for two days. The console's status screen still said up, with a stale 80% signal, and only the console's own health checks knew the truth. Nothing had needed the backup yet, so nobody else knew either.
ux.p2: So the driver reads the health checks now, and a dead backup reads down. That's the whole reason this integration exists: you find out on a Monday afternoon, not the night the fiber gets cut.
ux.h2b: Network first, then everything that hangs off it.
ux.o1b: Every adopted device, switch port, PoE draw, and internet (WAN) link, and which WAN is carrying traffic, as tags that sync themselves. A switch adopted tomorrow shows up by itself, and one that disappears goes bad quality instead of vanishing out from under its alarms. Read on real consoles.
ux.o2b: Clients keyed by MAC, never IP, because the controller shows addresses a machine left hours ago. Mark a network as OT (your control network), accept what is on it, and anything new raises an alarm. Link a PLC to its switch port once, and when it goes quiet it tells you which port and whether the link is up. Tested against a lab controller and read on real consoles.
ux.o3b: An overview with a WAN strip that goes amber when the site is running on the backup link, and a topology map laid out the same way every time, so nothing jiggles on a wall board. The map zooms to eight times and pinches on a touch screen. Click a switch, see which lines on the Plant tree it feeds. Switch faceplates show a port's traffic as a trace, WAN latency gets one too, and one button makes the usual alarms: device offline, uplink down, gateway on its backup, and PoE over a limit you give. A WAN throughput trace is not built yet.
ux.o4b: The controller's live event feed, so a switch dropping off shows up in seconds and lands in the logbook. Polling stays the truth: if the live feed dies you lose speed, never correctness. Events are filed under the switch or access point they are about, and an AI agent can ask for the topology and the console's latest events. A client joining reached the logbook six seconds after the cable went in.
ux.o5b: The locate LED, a device restart, a switch port's PoE power cycle and PoE mode, a wireless network on or off, and a client block, every one through the write gate and off until you arm that tag. A power cycle waits out a 15 minute cooldown, and a port that carries the network is never cycled. Proven on a lab controller and one real access point. Shutting the port an unknown device just showed up on is not built yet.
ux.o6b: Cameras as entities with detections as triggers and a snapshot on the alarm that pages you. Door events in the logbook and unlock behind the gate. Outlet power feeding the energy numbers. Each one ships after it has run on real gear, not before.
ux.h2c: A protocol driver, not a side system.
ux.p3: A UniFi console is a device in HotLoop, same as a PLC, and its switches, ports, and WAN links are tags. That one decision means alarms, trends, entities, rules, the audit, OPC UA, and AI agents all work on your network the day the driver does, without building half of each again for one vendor.
ux.c1b: One session per console, reused for every read, so a console never locks HotLoop out for logging in too often.
ux.c1d: One session per console, reused for every read, with a limit on how often it signs in. If a console does lock it out, HotLoop waits the lockout out instead of making it longer.
ux.c2b: You confirm the console's identity once, and a console with a different key is refused before your password is sent.
ux.c2d: The first connect stops on purpose and shows you the console's key fingerprint. Check it, confirm it. From then on a console with a different key is refused before your password goes anywhere.
ux.c3b: Which WAN is carrying traffic, as a tag you can alarm on. Know the plant failed over to the backup link before the data bill tells you.
ux.c4b: HotLoop won't cycle an uplink, or the port powering the backup WAN, no matter who asks. Worked out from the topology, not typed in.
ux.c4d: HotLoop won't cycle an uplink, or the port powering the backup WAN, no matter who asks. Worked out from the topology, not typed in by hand, so nobody forgets one.
ux.c5b: A port can't be power-cycled twice in fifteen minutes. A rule that cycles a PLC every two minutes is how you cook a power supply.
ux.c5d: Fifteen minutes per port. A rule that cycles a PLC every two minutes is how you cook a power supply, and one that needs more than one cycle has a problem a cycle won't fix.
ux.c6b: No VLANs, firewall rules, DHCP, static IPs, SSIDs, or firmware. That's the UniFi app's job. HotLoop does the few things an operator needs at 2am.
ux.c6d: No VLANs, firewall rules, DHCP, static IPs, SSIDs, or firmware. We've watched a switch lose its controller over one static IP change. That's the UniFi app's job. HotLoop does the few things an operator needs at 2am.
ux.p4: Console passwords are entered in HotLoop and stored encrypted, with the key kept outside the database, so a dump or a backup doesn't hand anybody the keys to your network.

cy.title: HotLoop for CODESYS: screens and alarms for a PLC
cy.desc: HotLoop beside a CODESYS runtime: screens and alarms read through its OPC UA server, nothing installed in CODESYS. Chart {version}, from the App Store or Helm.
cy.ogAlt: HotLoop for CODESYS, the screens and alarms for a CODESYS PLC.
cy.h1: The screen for your CODESYS PLC, and a second set of eyes on it.
cy.lede: HotLoop for CODESYS runs HotLoop on the same node as a CODESYS runtime. It reads the PLC's variables through the runtime's own OPC UA server, puts them on screens that work on a panel PC, a phone, or a wall, and raises alarms on them. Nothing is installed in CODESYS and nothing writes to the PLC. The consequence: the operators get a screen, and the PLC gets a second set of eyes that doesn't depend on anything else on the node.
cy.btnLineup: See the rest of the lineup
cy.h2a: Screens, alarms, and a PLC that never knows we are there.
cy.lede1: The screens are drawn outside the runtime, over the OPC UA server the runtime already has. So a change to a screen is a HotLoop edit, not a download to the PLC, and the same screen is on the panel PC and on a phone.
cy.d1h: It reads the PLC the documented way.
cy.d1p: Through the runtime's own OPC UA server, with HotLoop's CODESYS connector. Nothing is installed in CODESYS, so there is nothing in the runtime to patch.
cy.d1l: CODESYS documents one way for a third party to read a controller's variables, and it is the runtime's own OPC UA server. The PLC publishes what you want seen with a Symbol Configuration in the IDE, and HotLoop reads those variables by the names the programmer gave them, like Application.GVL_Line.rTemp, not by a node id. The Symbol Configuration is the only change to the PLC project, so your program stays yours.
cy.d2p: HotLoop dashboards: values, gauges, trends, and alarm lists, on a phone, a panel PC, or a wall, with one layout that folds down to a phone.
cy.d2l: These are the dashboards every HotLoop product has. A dashboard can be handed to the roles that need it or bound to one physical screen, which opens full bleed with bigger touch targets. A card commands nothing by itself.
cy.d3p: ISA-18.2 alarms on the PLC's variables, including the one that cleared before anybody saw it, so a trip that fixed itself is still on the list at shift change.
cy.d4p: HotLoop runs beside the runtime on the same node, with its own database and nothing else in the path.
cy.d4m: If the runtime stops answering, every tag reads bad with the reason, never zero, and HotLoop reconnects by itself.
cy.d4l: A restart of the runtime, or a new program loaded, drops the session. The device goes disconnected, every tag reads bad with the reason "the PLC's runtime is not answering", and HotLoop reconnects with backoff and reads the symbols as they now are. In the lab that took about a minute and a half from a runtime restart to good values again.
cy.h2b: A real run, with made-up plant labels.
cy.lede2: This is HotLoop Edge reading a real CODESYS runtime. The PLC program is HotLoop's own lab program, so the numbers are the lab's, and the labels (Line 2, Mixer temperature, Riverside Bottling) are ours, put there by the profile. It is HotLoop's default interface, and light or dark follows your system.
cy.s1Alt: The Line 2 screen: four value cards, a gauge, a fifteen minute trend of the mixer temperature, and an alarm list with one alarm
cy.s1Cap: The screen the profile makes: values, a gauge, a trend, and the alarm list. Everything on it reads from the PLC through the runtime's OPC UA server.
cy.s2Alt: The alarm list with Mixer temperature high, marked returned to normal and unacknowledged
cy.s2Cap: An alarm that cleared on its own before anybody saw it stays on the list, marked as returned to normal and unacknowledged, so a trip that fixed itself is still there at shift change.
cy.s3Alt: The Devices screen with one CODESYS device, six tags, connected
cy.s3Cap: The device the setup made: a CODESYS device, six tags, connected.
cy.s4Alt: The Line 2 screen on a phone, in one column
cy.s4AltD: The Line 2 screen on a phone, in dark
cy.s4Cap: The same screen on a phone. One layout folds from twelve columns to one, so nobody builds the phone version.
cy.h2c: Four refusals, and each one is on purpose.
cy.w1h: It won't write to your PLC.
cy.w1p: Every tag it sets up is read-only, and the profile marks none writable.
cy.w1m: A person can arm a tag later, one at a time, and then the write gate and the PLC's own symbol rights both get a say.
cy.w2h: It won't put anything in the runtime.
cy.w2p: No library, no task, no function block, no agent.
cy.w2m: The runtime keeps doing its scan, and the only thing the PLC project needs is a Symbol Configuration that publishes the variables.
cy.w3h: It won't need a database pod.
cy.w3p: SQLite on the node's own storage. One file, and nothing else on the node that can fail on its own schedule.
cy.w4h: It won't lose its screens to a bad link.
cy.w4p: The screens keep running on a node that loses its link to the cluster, and that is built into the chart. The table below says what was tested.
cy.lede4: Four parts, and each says how it was tested. The table further down names what was run.
cy.b1p: HotLoop's CODESYS driver: read and discover by symbol, with arrays and structures walked into one point per field.
cy.b1l: It lists what the application exports as the types it has: a STRING is a string, a TIME is milliseconds, an enumeration is an integer. An array lists its first elements, and any element can still be addressed by its symbol. It shapes every request to the limits the runtime publishes, so a big program never overwhelms it. It was tested against a real CODESYS runtime and on bare metal (2026-11-17).
cy.b2p: HotLoop Edge with defaults for a runtime on a node: SQLite, and the parts you do not need beside a PLC switched off.
cy.b3p: A small program that applies a profile to HotLoop and keeps it right: the device, the variables, the alarms, and one screen.
cy.b3l: The profile is one file the installer provides, never part of the chart or the image, so both are generic. A variable the PLC gained since is added, one it lost reads bad with the server's reason, and the screen and alarms are replaced only when the profile's revision is higher, so a change a person made survives until a newer profile is shipped on purpose.
cy.b4p: People sign in from the EmberCORE dashboard, and HotLoop for CODESYS inherits it.
cy.b4l: A valid sign-in from the dashboard puts a person in as an operator or an admin, and a wrong app, a wrong tenant, an expired sign-in, or a tampered one is refused. Local sign-in still works for setup.
cy.h2e: From the App Store on EmberNet, or with Helm.
cy.lede5: It needs a CODESYS runtime on the same node with its OPC UA server on, and a Symbol Configuration in the PLC program for the variables you want to see. The chart wraps HotLoop Edge and is public, so you can pull it with no login.
cy.helmP: The profile is one small file: the device, the variables to keep, the alarms, and the screen. Want HotLoop alone, to set up by hand? Switch the automatic setup off with one option.
cy.enP: On EmberNet it is an App Store app that the EmberNet team installs on your tenant, and the Store writes the profile for you…
cy.enM: …so there is nothing to do afterward. Pick the node the runtime is on and it starts beside it.
cy.note5: The steps, the profile's shape, and the sign-in are on the install page in the docs. The chart is public, so your team can review it before anything is installed.
cy.h2f: What was run, so you don't find out at commissioning.
cy.t1: The device, its tags (none writable), its alarm, and its screen appeared with no hand step. Every value read good and moved. It came back after a restart. Through a runtime restart the install read bad with the reason "the PLC's runtime is not answering" and came back by itself about a minute and a half later.
cy.t2: A real CODESYS Control for Linux runtime running a lab program, with HotLoop Edge beside it on Kubernetes.
cy.t3: The pieces that had only been run in the lab, including a node losing its link to the cluster, were tested on bare metal (2026-11-17).
cy.note6: What comes next is on the roadmap.
cy.licH: It installs HotLoop Edge, so the same terms.
cy.licP: HotLoop for CODESYS is under the HotLoop Source License Agreement 1.0, and so is the HotLoop Edge it runs. It is free to use and source-available, not OSI open source. Home and lab use is free. For business use, talk to us.
fw.title: HotLoop Flow: a Node-RED alternative in Go
fw.desc: A Node-RED-compatible flow engine in one static Go binary, with bounded queues and a thread per node. Free for home and lab, and its source is public.
fw.ogAlt: HotLoop Flow, a flow engine in one static Go binary.
fw.h1: Wire the plant. Review it like code.
fw.lede: A flow engine for the plant floor, in one static Go binary with its own editor. Every deploy is a record you can diff and roll back, a trace shows where a message went, and a wire can ride out an outage. It reads your existing flows.json too, so you can bring what you have.
fw.nStrong: HotLoop Flow {version} is out. One odd value can no longer take your plant's Flow down, function nodes run await and promises, and all 62 of Node-RED's own example flows give what Node-RED gives. Nothing in your flows, settings or chart changes.
fw.nBody: The code is at github.com/HotLoop-io/hotloop-flow. It runs on amd64 and arm64, so every box pulls its own, and there is a chart for Kubernetes. Upgrading is a plain image bump, and the release notes say what each version changes before you do it. Flow is under the HotLoop Source License Agreement 1.0, and home and lab use is free.
fw.wh: Ship it, watch it, and let it ride out a bad hour.
fw.wlede: Each card is the short version. The full text for each is in the docs and the release notes.
fw.g1.h: Every deploy is a record, and a flow can be tested before it ships.
fw.g1.1b: Who, when, why, and the flow file byte for byte, with credentials encrypted as they stood. A diff reads node by node, and rollback redeploys an old record. "Who changed line 3 and put it back" is a command, not an archaeology project.
fw.g1.2b: A command line prints the diff and deploys against the revision it came from, so a race is a red pipeline. A pipeline holds a token that can read and deploy, nothing else.
fw.g1.3b: A test file runs on the real runtime. Turn on the gate and a deploy that fails the suite is refused with the whole report, so a broken flow never reaches the plant.
fw.g1.4b: A save restarts the nodes that changed. MQTT sessions, listeners and Delay queues on everything else keep running.
fw.g2.h: Click a message and see the path it took.
fw.g2.1b: The canvas lights up the path a message took, with timing and payload at every hop. Replay it into a draft of the flow, or turn the trace into a test.
fw.g2.2b: Every hop can go to your own observability collector as a span, with a bounded buffer, so tracing never becomes the outage.
fw.g2.3b: Metrics per node for your dashboards. Logins, deploys, refusals and rollbacks go to an audit log, each saying who, from where, and what.
fw.g3.h: A slow historian or a chatty sensor is a graph, not an outage.
fw.g3.1b: Every inbox has a ceiling and a policy per node: block, drop the newest, drop the oldest, or raise it to a Catch node. Every message that does not fit is counted.
fw.g3.2b: Mark a wire durable and, when the node behind it stops answering, messages go to disk in order and drain when it returns. We killed a real InfluxDB for ten minutes and no rows went missing or doubled.
fw.g3.3b: Flow, global and node context are kept on disk, so a restart no longer wipes them.
fw.g3.4b: Each node runs on its own lightweight thread. A CPU-heavy Function node costs you a core, not the editor and every other flow on the box.
fw.g4.h: Native nodes for the protocols a plant already runs.
fw.g4.1b: Modbus read and write, and OPC UA read, subscribe, and write.
fw.g4.2b: Read and write for Siemens and Allen-Bradley controllers, tested on bare metal (2026-11-17). A new controller is still a commissioning job, so check a value you already know.
fw.g4.3b: As an edge node and as a host, checked in both directions and against a real broker.
fw.g4.4b: MQTT 5 with properties and the last will, TLS, HTTP request and MQTT, and Inject on a crontab that fires when Node-RED's would.
fw.g5.l: Reach the rest of the plant
fw.g5.h: Talk to HotLoop, let an AI agent call a flow, and catch a wrong-shaped message early.
fw.g5.1b: Follow HotLoop's live feed, read state, run scripts, and apply recipes. The write nodes can send through HotLoop's write gate, and a refused write never reaches the equipment.
fw.g5.2b: A flow can serve itself to an AI agent as a tool, and a flow can call tools on any other agent server. A token is required, and every call is audited under the caller.
fw.g5.3b: A plugin is a signed, sandboxed file, not a package pulled from the internet. Unsigned ones refuse to load, and with no trusted keys nothing loads at all.
fw.g5.4h: Typed wires and the Inject check
fw.g5.4b: Give the json node a schema and a wrong-shaped value goes to Catch with every bad field named. A deploy is refused when two ends of a wire can never agree.
fw.g6.h: A second way to run a tab, for test benches and data loggers, with 37 node types of its own beside the ones for messages.
fw.g6.1h: Diagrams with loops and an error wire
fw.g6.1b: In a diagram each node runs once, when every wired input has a value, and nodes with no wire between them run at the same time. While and for loops carry a value from one pass to the next, and an error travels on a wire of its own. Existing flows run exactly as they did.
fw.g6.2b: A panel with controls, indicators and charts that opens on a phone, and a run bar with highlight execution, probes, breakpoints and step.
fw.g6.3b: Statistics, integral, derivative and filter nodes, a node that reads NI hardware, a durable MQTT output, and a TDMS log you can open in NI's tools.
fw.g7.h: It refuses to start without a login in front of it.
fw.g7.1h: No login is a startup error
fw.g7.1b: Turning authentication off takes a deliberate setting, and the editor wears a no-login badge while it is off.
fw.g7.2b: Two-factor sign-in is free. Five wrong passwords lock an account from that address for fifteen minutes, and sessions survive a restart.
fw.g7.3b: Credentials are encrypted with modern, authenticated encryption, and deploy records never hand them out, encrypted or not.
fw.g7.4b: The exec node ships disabled until an operator allows specific commands, with no shell. File nodes are fenced to the volume.
fw.g7.5h: A sandbox with nothing to reach
fw.g7.5b: The Function node runs with no access to the host, no files, and no network. Plugins run signed, with a memory ceiling and a timeout.
fw.g7.6b: A 41.7 MB self-contained program that idles at about 16 MiB and answers its first request in 0.05 s. It runs on a Raspberry Pi 5.
fw.eh: Wire it, review it, follow a message down the wires.
fw.elede: Light or dark, it follows your system. These are real screenshots of the running editor on an oven line with two deployments behind it, retaken when the editor changes.
fw.e1a: The Flow editor on an oven line: the canvas, the deployment history, and the debug and runtime panels
fw.e1d: The Flow editor on an oven line, in dark
fw.e1c: The canvas is what's running. The debug dock and the Runtime table under it say what every node is doing.
fw.e2a: The review panel listing one changed node, with a note box, beside the canvas with that node outlined
fw.e2c: Deploy shows the change on the canvas and in words, and asks for a note that lands in the history.
fw.e3a: A traced message lit across the canvas with the time each node spent on it, and the debug dock below
fw.e3c: Click Trace on a debug line and the path that message took lights up, hop by hop.
fw.e4e: What a runtime says when the dashboard signs people in and the page was opened another way
fw.e4c: Flow won't start unlocked. When the EmberCORE dashboard signs people in, a runtime opened any other way says to come in through the dashboard.
fw.ih: One image, one volume, and an admin account before it will start.
fw.ilede: Flow refuses to run unlocked, so every install sets an admin password and a credential secret first. Keep the credential secret somewhere that is not the box: every broker and database password Flow stores is unreadable without it, which is the point.
fw.podP: One image, one volume, and a few lines to set the admin account. Service files that follow the stable release, and the full steps, are on the install page.
fw.k8sP: The chart makes the admin password and the credential secret on first install and keeps them on every upgrade. One release is one instance, on purpose.
fw.nh: A 41.7 MB program that answers in 0.05 s, with the limits stated up front.
fw.nlede: Measured on a desktop Linux machine, three runs of each command, and the range is what's printed. Flow prints absolute numbers only, because a side-by-side table moves every time the box changes and ends up describing the box more than Flow. You can run the same benchmark on your own hardware.
fw.b3: Start to answering its first request
fw.b6: Web requests through a five-node flow
fw.v7: under half a millisecond / a few milliseconds
fw.pi5p: The same flow and the same commands, running the published arm64 image on one Pi 5 with 8 GB. Three runs, and the range is what's printed.
fw.p7v: about half a millisecond / under 3 milliseconds
fw.pi5n: The ten minute row is the honest one for a box that stays loaded: the board heated up and throttled its clock, and Flow still held steady. Idle memory runs higher than the desktop figure above, and the method is in the bench docs.
fw.cvI: Four notes on what the numbers measure.
fw.cv1: The web number includes the whole web stack, on purpose, since that is what a client of your flow sees. It is not a scheduler benchmark. The engine row is the scheduler, with no I/O in the path.
fw.cv2: The tail moves more than the median. Under saturation every runtime queues, and queueing owns the worst case, so it wanders between runs while the typical latency barely does.
fw.cv3: The engine's peak memory is a burst, not a resting state. That row fires 200,000 messages at once and the bounded inboxes hold the rest back. Feed it at a sensor's pace and memory sits where the idle rows say.
fw.cv4: A desktop is not a Pi. The Pi 5 is measured above. The image has grown over the releases as the plant nodes, tracing, the state store, the HotLoop and agent nodes, schema checking, plugins and FlowLab came in.
fw.cvF: Memory is the process's own resident memory, not what a container tool charges the container, so the figure is the same whichever tool reads it.
fw.hh: The same flow file on both runtimes.
fw.hlede: We deployed the same five-node flow file to Flow and to the latest Node-RED, unchanged, and ran the same load on the same machine in the same sitting. Flow came out smaller, faster and quicker to start. The table and every condition behind it are below.
fw.hDetail: The table and every caveat behind it
fw.hcH: Three things that table does not say.
fw.hc1: Cold start includes roughly two seconds of container start that both runtimes pay, so the real gap between the two programs is smaller than that row implies.
fw.hc2: The throughput figure includes the whole web stack, on purpose, since that is the only surface both present identically. It is not a measurement of either scheduler in isolation.
fw.hc3: The worst-case gap is far narrower than the typical gap. Under saturation both runtimes queue, queueing dominates the tail, and the median is the only column where per-request cost actually shows up.
fw.hn1: Two more notes. The throughput, latency and cold start rows are from a run on 2026-08-08, on an earlier build of Flow, so don't divide them by the newer absolute numbers above. The image row is the current image against the Node-RED image from that run. When we ran it, Flow was 25.1 MB and the gap was 29×, and Flow has grown since as it gained features.
fw.hn2: Memory isn't in this table, on purpose. Those numbers came off a container tool that reports what the kernel charges the container, not what the process holds, and nobody could reproduce them. A ratio across two methods is exactly the mistake that got the old numbers pulled.
fw.nrlede: Flow reads your existing flows.json and runs it on a runtime built for the plant floor: a bounded queue on every wire, a thread for every node, a Function node sealed off from the host, and authenticated encryption on stored credentials. The migration guide walks a flow across, and the compatibility table below lists every node and every difference. Community nodes are the one thing that doesn't come along, because they need Node.js.
fw.l1b: Every inbox is bounded, with a policy per node: block, drop the newest, drop the oldest, or raise it to a Catch node. A chatty sensor and a slow database can't run the box out of memory.
fw.l2b: Each node runs on its own thread, in order within the node and in parallel across nodes, so one CPU-heavy Function node never freezes the editor or another flow.
fw.l3h: A Function node sealed off from the host.
fw.l3b: Function code runs with no access to the host, its files or the network.
fw.l4b: Stored credentials use modern authenticated encryption under a proper key derivation, so a file somebody altered fails to decrypt.
fw.nd1b: Node-RED, by default, hands every message to the next node through a queue, and nothing puts a ceiling on that queue. A fast source outruns a slow sink, the queue grows, and the pod runs out of memory and gets killed with nothing in the log to explain it. Every inbox in Flow is bounded, with a policy per node: block, drop the newest, drop the oldest, or raise it to a Catch node and let the flow decide.
fw.nd2b: One event loop carries the runtime, the editor API, the websocket fan-out, and every node's I/O. One CPU-heavy Function node stalls all of it, including the editor you are using to find out why it stalled. In Flow, every node instance gets its own thread, ordered within a node and parallel across nodes.
fw.nd3h: The Function node's sandbox is not a boundary.
fw.nd3b: Node-RED's Function node runs your code in node:vm. That is not our accusation, it is Node's own documentation: “The node:vm module is not a security mechanism. Do not use it to run untrusted code.” Node-RED's own guide says an unsecured editor is only suitable on a trusted network, and anyone who can deploy a flow can run commands on the box, which is fine on a Pi in a workshop and not fine on a customer's plant floor. It is not hypothetical either: CVE-2025-41656 is unauthenticated remote command execution, rated critical, in Pilz's IndustrialPI 4 firmware, because authentication for the Node-RED server on it was not configured by default. That is a CVE in Pilz's product, not in Node-RED, and Node-RED's own guide says the editor is not secured by default.
fw.nd4b: They are encrypted with AES-256-CTR keyed by a raw SHA-256 of your secret. CTR has no MAC, so anyone who can write the credentials file on a shared volume can flip chosen plaintext bits, which turns “can write a file” into “can change a broker password to one they picked.” And plain SHA-256 is not a key derivation function. There is no CVE on either of those, and both are still real.
fw.ch: The same idea, built for production.
fw.d1b: Every node on its own thread
fw.d2a: None, the queue grows until the box dies
fw.d3a: Branches can quietly corrupt each other
fw.d3b: Every recipient gets its own copy
fw.d4a: Not a security boundary, by its own docs
fw.d4b: Locked in a box with no access to the host
fw.d5a: Packages that run inside the same process
fw.d5b: Signed, sandboxed plugins, refused unless the key is trusted
fw.d6a: Any command, through a shell by default
fw.d6b: Off until you allow specific commands, and no shell at all
fw.d7a: Any path the process can reach
fw.d9b: Get, set, and safe counters and updates
fw.d10b: Written safely, with three backups deep
fw.d14a: Two hand-written files that must match
fw.cAfter: Flow is deliberately not identical. Node-RED hands the first recipient on a wire the original message and only clones for the rest, so two branches that each think they own their message can quietly corrupt each other, and which one breaks depends on the order you wired them. Every recipient in Flow gets its own copy. A small message costs 411 to 453 ns to copy. A 1 MiB binary payload would cost 128 to 156 µs per recipient, so those travel shared and immutable instead, at 250 to 279 ns, which is exactly where copying would have hurt. Every deliberate difference is written down in the compatibility matrix, so none of them is a surprise on a live line.
fw.kh: {n} node types, and each one says how close it is to Node-RED.
fw.klede: A node that is partially compatible and silent about how is worse than one that is obviously absent, because the flow appears to work and quietly does the wrong thing. So a test fails the build if a node does not say what is missing.
fw.k1p: Behaves as the Node-RED node of the same type does.
fw.k2p: A subset. The notes say exactly which parts are missing.
fw.k3p: Deliberately different, and the notes say why.
fw.k5h: Not supported at all: community nodes
fw.k5p: They are npm packages that need Node.js, so they don't run in Flow. The plant nodes most flows lean on run natively.
fw.k6h: JSONata, checked against the published examples
fw.k6p: Every jsonata property runs on our own JSONata engine, which passes 1,673 of the 1,686 published test cases. The 13 misses are listed in the repository.
fw.rh: Release notes, the roadmap and the migration guide.
fw.sh: Running today, with the roadmap in the open.
fw.slede: Verified against a real MQTT broker, InfluxDB and PostgreSQL, and on bare metal. Here's what's still in progress, so you can plan around it. The full plan is on the Flow roadmap.
fw.n1b: Modbus TCP, OPC UA, S7, EtherNet/IP, and Sparkplug B nodes ran against simulators, a real broker, and bare metal (2026-11-17). Next: Modbus RTU, Modbus over TLS, OPC UA events, history, method calls and browse, S7 timers and counters, and PCCC controllers.
fw.n2b: Flows can follow HotLoop's live feed, read state, run scripts, and apply recipes, and the write nodes can go through HotLoop's write gate. Next: an https HotLoop with a private CA.
fw.n3b: Flows serve tools to agents and call tools on other servers. Next: OAuth, stdio servers, resources, prompts, sampling, and a tool's output schema.
fw.n4b: Signed, sandboxed plugins are out and were run on bare metal (2026-11-17).
fw.n5b: Rebuilt in HotLoop's colors and type, with browser tests that pass in Chrome.
fw.n6b: A plant runs it through EmberNet today, and everything past the deploy line was proven against simulators and on bare metal.

For business use, talk to us. Each version converts to AGPL-3.0 or later four years after its release. The Flow repository is public, so you can read all of it.
wg.heading: Go on, try to move a machine.
wg.intro: press-01/Setpoint, range 0 to 250 degC, sitting at 210. Everything ships locked, so your first try is going to bounce. Unlock it one switch at a time and watch where it stops.
wg.empty: Nothing yet. Every attempt lands here, refused or not.
wg.foot: A simulation in your browser. The checks, their order, and what they refuse are the Gateway's own.
wg.s1p: A signed-in person needs the permission to write, and a viewer does not have it. An agent needs its token, or it is turned away.
wg.s1m: A viewer who tries is stopped at the door, and the day somebody hands the wrong role to the wrong person, the write still doesn't happen.
wg.s2m: There is one master switch, and it has always shipped off, because a fresh install that can move machinery before anybody decided it should is a lawsuit with a web UI.
wg.s3p: Agents get their own switch, checked only for an agent. It narrows the master switch and can never open a door the master switch closed.
wg.s4p: Every tag is read-only until somebody marks it writable, one at a time, on purpose. Import 4,000 tags and none of them is armed.
wg.s5p: Out of range is refused, never clamped. Somebody who typed 500 on a 0 to 250 setpoint made a mistake, and quietly sending 250 means they never find out.
wg.s6p: A write through an entity adds the entity's own rules: a number's step, a text's pattern, an entity somebody disabled.
wg.s6m: They're checked here, so that refusal is audited like any other.
wg.s7p: No running device, no write, and the refusal is audited. A dry run checks the live connection itself, so a recipe or a script finds out before anything moves.
wg.s8h: The audit row is written, then the value goes out.
wg.s8p: In that order. A refusal is recorded as a refusal, and a write that hangs or crashes the process still left evidence that it was attempted.
wg.rWrites: writes are disabled on this deployment.
wg.rArmed: this tag is not marked writable.
wg.skipCheck: Straight to a tag. No entity rules to add.
wg.aDoor: The gate never heard about it, so there is nothing to audit.
wg.vOk: Written. {v} degC went to press-01, and the audit has who, from where, and the 210 it replaced.
wg.vDoor: Bounced at the door. The Board still shows a viewer the value. It just never offers them a Write button.
wg.vRef: {why} The audit got a row anyway, because somebody hammering a tag they can't touch is exactly what an engineer wants to find next week.
bz.heading: Pull the wire on TT-101.
bz.intro: Same sensor, same moment, two systems. Low alarm at {lo} degC. Pull the wire and watch which one wakes somebody up for nothing.
bz.aNaive: Trend where a failed read is recorded as zero
bz.aHl: Trend where a failed read is marked bad quality
bz.held: Normal, held. The reading is bad, so the alarm isn't evaluated on it.
bz.verdict: The left one just paged somebody at 3am for a process event that never happened. The right one told the truth: nobody knows the temperature right now, and the problem is the instrument, not the tank.
bz.foot: A simulation in your browser. The quality rule and the held alarm are the Gateway's.
bp.heading: Turn the sensor up and watch who dies.
bp.intro: One sensor, one database insert that can take 100 messages a second. Push the sensor past that and the difference between the two runtimes stops being a table row.
bp.oom: OOMKilled. Exit code 137. The log says nothing about why.
bp.growing: Queue growing with no ceiling. Memory follows it.
bp.sBlock: Inbox full, so the sender waits for room, up to blockTimeout. The pressure goes upstream, not into memory.
bp.sNewest: Inbox full, so each arriving message is dropped, counted and announced.
bp.sOldest: Inbox full, so the oldest queued message makes room for the newest. The sink always gets fresh values.
bp.sError: Inbox full, so each send that does not fit goes to a Catch node, and the flow decides.
bp.v1: At this rate nobody is in trouble. Push the sensor past 100 a second.
bp.v2: Node-RED is buffering the difference in memory. Give it a few seconds.
bp.v3: Node-RED never dropped a message. It dropped {n} of them at once, with the pod. Flow made you choose what gets lost, ahead of time, and it is still running.
bp.foot: A simulation in your browser, with a second of it standing in for a minute on the plant. Flow's inbox size and its four policies are the real ones. The memory figures are illustrative. The shape of the failure is not.
