int.label: Integrations
int.h1: What it speaks, and how far each one has been proven.
int.lede: Twelve native drivers (the connections to your PLCs and devices) on the Gateway and {nodes} node types in Flow. Each driver lists the systems it has run against and what to check at commissioning, so your first day with it holds no surprises.
int.nTitle: S7comm (Siemens) and EtherNet/IP have run on bare metal (2026-11-17).
int.nBody: As with any new controller, confirm a value you already know at commissioning.
int.nodesLede: Generated from Flow's node registry. A node that is anything short of full has to say what is different, and the build fails if one does not.
int.same: Behaves as the Node-RED node does.
int.fine: These rows are imported from Flow's generated compatibility document. Node type strings are shown exactly as they appear in a flow file. Two of them, the InfluxDB and PostgreSQL config nodes, were renamed with the product to hotloop-flow-influxdb and hotloop-flow-postgres, and the old emberwire- names are not kept as aliases. A flow saved by version 0.1.0 that uses either one has to be pointed at the new name.
int.pTitleGm: PROFINET, HART and DNP3 through HotLoop Gateway
wo.p: A float32 spans two 16-bit registers, and vendors disagree about which comes first. Type the two registers exactly as the device sent them. Only one of the four results below is the truth, and nothing on the wire tells you which.
wo.err: Enter one to four hexadecimal digits in each box.
pr.opc-ua.va2: Independent OPC UA servers in two languages
pr.opc-ua.sum: Prefer this one when a device offers a choice. It browses, it is properly secured, and it subscribes.
pr.opc-ua.b1: The driver subscribes rather than polls. The server sends a value when it changes, at a rate it can sustain, instead of being asked the same question every scan by a client with no idea whether anything moved. If a server refuses a subscription, the driver falls back to batched reads rather than failing the device.
pr.opc-ua.b2: Addresses use the stable name of a node, not its position, so a server reload or a firmware upgrade never quietly points a tag at the wrong thing. A typo is caught when you save it, not three weeks later when a tag reads bad forever.
pr.opc-ua.trap: A node's position number depends on the order the server loaded things. Add a namespace or upgrade firmware and position 3 quietly becomes something else, so every reading is wrong with no error anywhere. HotLoop addresses by name so that can't happen to you.
pr.modbus.sum: The 1979 workhorse. PLCs, VFDs, power meters, RTUs, and the fallback of every gateway that has nothing better.
pr.modbus.b1: All four word orders are supported, under the names vendor manuals print: ABCD, CDAB, BADC, and DCBA. Set a device default and override it per tag.
pr.modbus.b2: Addressing follows your drawings: if they use the traditional 40001-style numbering, one setting lets you write the numbers straight from them. Getting this wrong by one is the oldest Modbus bug there is.
pr.modbus.b3: Reads are merged into blocks, so neighboring registers become one request and a busy serial line gets some peace.
pr.modbus.b4: Writing a single bit of a holding register keeps the other fifteen bits intact, because Modbus has no atomic bit-set there.
pr.modbus.trap: Word order is the setting people get wrong, and a float read with the wrong order is not obviously wrong on a screen. It is a plausible number that is not the truth.
pr.mqtt-sparkplug.va1: Eclipse Mosquitto, with crafted Sparkplug frames
pr.mqtt-sparkplug.sum: Plain MQTT, or Sparkplug B as a full primary host application.
pr.mqtt-sparkplug.b1: As a Sparkplug B primary host, the driver does the things the specification asks for and most integrations skip.
pr.mqtt-sparkplug.b2: Edge nodes can see the host drop instead of guessing from a timeout. The host tracks every node's sequence, asks a node to re-announce itself when it skips or after the host's own reconnect, and matches a death to the right birth, so a stale death certificate from a previous session can't kill the current one.
pr.mqtt-sparkplug.trap: Delivering Sparkplug messages concurrently reorders them, which makes a healthy node look like it is dropping messages and provokes a storm of re-announcements. HotLoop keeps message order.
pr.ethernet-ip.va1: Address, batching, and type-mapping tests on CIP frames
pr.ethernet-ip.sum: Allen-Bradley ControlLogix, CompactLogix, and Micro820. Tags have names, so the controller can be asked what it holds.
pr.ethernet-ip.b1: The data type comes from the tag, or from an explicit suffix, which wins.
pr.ethernet-ip.b2: Reads are batched, falling back to single reads when a batch fails, so one bad tag path does not blind the other nineteen.
pr.ethernet-ip.trap: The controller rejects a read whose declared type does not match, so the type has to come from somewhere. Unknown falls back to a REAL, which most process values are.
pr.ethernet-ip.nvn: Check a value you already know on the controller at commissioning before trusting a screen.
pr.s7comm.sum: Siemens S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200, and S7-1500, over ISO-on-TCP by rack and slot.
pr.s7comm.b1: Defaults suit an S7-1200 or S7-1500, and an S7-300 or S7-400 usually needs one setting changed.
pr.s7comm.b2: HotLoop uses the plain connection type, so it does not occupy the connection an engineer wants for TIA Portal.
pr.s7comm.b3: There is no browse: a CPU does not publish the layout of its data blocks, because that lives in the TIA Portal project.
pr.s7comm.trap: The type is required for anything wider than a byte. The protocol cannot tell you whether four bytes are a REAL or a DINT, because that is a fact about the PLC program, not about the wire.
pr.s7comm.nvn: Check a value you already know on the PLC at commissioning before trusting a screen. Set the type of anything wider than a byte from the PLC program.
pr.mtconnect.va1: Golden MTConnect agent documents, served by a test HTTP server
pr.mtconnect.sum: Read-only machine tool telemetry. MTConnect has no command channel, so this driver reads only.
pr.mtconnect.b1: Two details separate a working integration from a plausible one. First, UNAVAILABLE becomes bad quality rather than a string or a zero. Second, a Condition's meaning is its state (Normal, Warning, Fault, or Unavailable), not its text, which is usually empty.
pr.mtconnect.b2: Browse walks the machine's whole component tree to any depth, so you pick data points instead of typing paths.
pr.mtconnect.trap: UNAVAILABLE is the agent explicitly saying it has no reading. It becomes bad quality, not the text "UNAVAILABLE" and not zero.
pr.mtconnect.nvn: Compare a value on the machine's own display with what HotLoop reads, at commissioning.
pr.http-rest.va1: Recorded JSON documents, served by a test HTTP server
pr.http-rest.sum: The catch-all, for energy meters, environmental sensors, OEM controllers, and the REST side of a gateway that speaks something proprietary underneath.
pr.http-rest.b1: One request serves every tag on the device. Browse walks the document and reports every value with the path that reaches it.
pr.http-rest.trap: These APIs love returning an unordered array of name and value objects, and indexing by position is a bug waiting for a firmware update. Select by field value instead.
pr.http-rest.nvn: Compare one value from the device's API with the device's own reading, at commissioning.
pr.unifi.va1: Real UniFi consoles, logged in as a view-only account
pr.unifi.va2: Real UniFi switches and a backup WAN
pr.unifi.sum: The plant network as a device: switches, ports, PoE, WAN failover and clients as tags, plus commands you arm to restart, power-cycle or block.
pr.unifi.b1: One login per console, reused for every read, and never more than one read every ten seconds whatever the poll interval says. Make a local account on the console, because a Ubiquiti cloud account can't sign in from a script. View-only is enough to read, and commands need a local Administrator.
pr.unifi.b2: The console's certificate is pinned. You confirm its identity once, and a console with a different key is refused before the password goes anywhere.
pr.unifi.b3: Switches, ports, PoE draw, WAN links, clients, and the site's health come in as tags that create themselves as gear is adopted, and go bad quality instead of vanishing. A switch dropping off is in the logbook when it happens.
pr.unifi.b4: It reads the whole network and it acts on it. Restart a device, power-cycle a PoE port, set a port's PoE mode, or block a client and let it back in. Each command is created read-only and is sent only after a person arms it through the write gate. A port is power-cycled at most once in 15 minutes, and an uplink port is never cycled. The screens, the topology map and the events are on the UniFi page.
pr.unifi.trap: A WAN block can say up with a stale signal while the backup link has been unplugged for days. The driver reads the console's own health checks instead, so a dead backup reads down.
pr.snmp.va1: A standard SNMP agent, read over v1, v2c, and v3 at every security level, on UDP and TCP
pr.snmp.sum: Switches, UPSs, PDUs, power meters, and any Linux box running snmpd, read-only. HotLoop never sends a SET.
pr.snmp.b1: Read-only, always. HotLoop never sends an SNMP SET, because a SET can change a switch's configuration, and the point of this driver is to see the plant network, not to run it.
pr.snmp.b2: There is no default community, because "public" is how a plant's switches get read by whoever asks. The community and the v3 passphrases are stored encrypted like every other device secret.
pr.snmp.b3: Counters report what the agent sent, and uptime is scaled to seconds for you. An object the agent does not have is a bad reading with the reason, and the others in the same request still read.
pr.snmp.b4: Point HotLoop at a device and it asks what it needs, looks at the real device, and keeps the points you choose, with nothing armed.
pr.snmp.trap: A wrong community answers with nothing. An SNMPv1 or v2c agent drops a request carrying a community it does not know, so a wrong community, a wrong port, a firewall, and an agent that is down all look like a timeout. HotLoop's message names all four. SNMPv3 does tell them apart.
pr.bacnet.va1: An independent BACnet stack serving every object type HotLoop reads
pr.bacnet.sum: Building controllers, meters, and thermostats on the IP network, read-only. HotLoop never writes a BACnet property.
pr.bacnet.b1: Read-only, on purpose. A BACnet write lands on a commandable output through a priority array, and a priority left set holds the equipment where it was put after whoever set it has gone home. That is a feature to design deliberately, not one to leave lying around.
pr.bacnet.b2: Connecting asks the device who it is. Set the device instance and a different device answering at a reused address, or a swapped controller, is refused instead of read.
pr.bacnet.b3: A device whose answer will not fit one frame is asked for fewer objects at a time, and an object that is not there fails its own tag and no other.
pr.bacnet.b4: Point HotLoop at a device and nothing it makes is armed.
pr.bacnet.trap: Status flags are part of the reading. An object whose fault flag is set reads bad, with the reason. One that is out of service or overridden reads uncertain, because its present value is something a person or a program put there, not a measurement.
pr.bacnet.nvn: A controller on an MS/TP trunk behind a BACnet router can't be reached directly. Address the router's own BACnet/IP side, or put a gateway in front. Vendors differ about their object lists and how they answer a request that is too big, so a new controller is still a commissioning job.
pr.bacnet.nvh: Tested against an independent BACnet stack, and on bare metal.
pr.codesys.va1: A real CODESYS Control for Linux runtime running a lab program, plus a program of over a hundred thousand variables read in about two seconds, reads and writes
pr.codesys.sum: A CODESYS PLC, read and written by the names its programmer gave the variables, through the runtime's own OPC UA server.
pr.codesys.b1: CODESYS documents one way for a third party to read a controller's variables, and it is the runtime's own OPC UA server, so that is what this driver uses. Nothing is installed in your PLC project beyond the Symbol Configuration.
pr.codesys.b2: Discovery lists what the application exports, with the types and the access the programmer gave them, and walks into arrays and structures.
pr.codesys.b3: A restart or a download drops the session. Every tag reads bad with the reason, and HotLoop reconnects by itself and reads the symbols as they are now. Requests are shaped to the limits the runtime publishes.
pr.codesys.trap: A PLC with no Symbol Configuration publishes nothing a client can read. The program has to export the variables you want, and a variable is writable from HotLoop only when its symbol is read and write. HotLoop's setup message says to add one.
pr.codesys.nvh: Tested against a real runtime, and on bare metal.
pr.opcua-pubsub.va1: An independent OPC UA stack, in both directions over multicast, in both encodings and with key and delta frames
pr.opcua-pubsub.va2: HotLoop Transmitter, publishing from inside a CODESYS PLC
pr.opcua-pubsub.sum: A publisher sends DataSets as UDP datagrams to whoever listens, unicast or multicast. HotLoop subscribes as a device and publishes as a setting.
pr.opcua-pubsub.b1: A lost message, a gap in the sequence numbers, marks that writer's tags uncertain until its next full update, because a change may have gone with it. A writer that goes silent reads bad, and a field the publisher marks bad or uncertain is that.
pr.opcua-pubsub.b2: Edge and the Gateway can also publish the tags you choose as OPC UA PubSub, switched off until you switch it on. A bad tag goes out as its status, never as its last value.
pr.opcua-pubsub.b3: The subscriber is read-only. HotLoop Transmitter is the publisher that runs inside a CODESYS PLC, and this is the driver that listens to it.
pr.opcua-pubsub.trap: A machine with more than one network card has to say which one joins the multicast group, or the join fails. Name the interface on the device.
pr.opcua-pubsub.nvn: Message security, chunking, discovery, events and structure fields are not supported. A datagram that uses one is refused by name, counted by reason, and never guessed at.
pr.opcua-pubsub.nvh: Tested in both directions against an independent stack, and against a CODESYS PLC.
pr.gateway-mode.sum: Eight protocols with no driver, by choice, reached through the gateway a site already has.
pr.gateway-mode.b1: PROFINET, EtherCAT, HART, DNP3, FINS, MELSEC/SLMP, CANopen, and FANUC FOCAS are not spoken natively, and there is no driver for them. That is a deliberate choice, not a gap waiting to be filled with a stub.
pr.gateway-mode.b2: Sites running these protocols almost always already have a gateway that re-publishes on OPC UA or Modbus, such as a PROFINET IO controller with an OPC UA server, or a HART multiplexer with a Modbus map. Point a device at that endpoint and configure it as OPC UA or Modbus.
pr.gateway-mode.b3: Eight more drivers that each duplicate what a site's existing gateway already does would be eight more things to get subtly wrong, on the equipment that is hardest to test against. If a site genuinely has no gateway and needs one of these natively, that is a real piece of work to schedule.
pr.gateway-mode.b4: There are no placeholder drivers. A protocol either has a working implementation or it is on this page.

ft.entities-and-the-equipment-tree.d: Every signal becomes a named thing that keeps its identity, on one plant tree. A motor is one entity built from the signals that make it up, so rules and agents talk about the pump, not a register number. Replace a PLC and your rules keep working.
ft.automations.d: Eleven kinds of trigger, entity state and the sun included, checked when you save. A broken rule dies in the editor, not at 3am halfway through a batch.
ft.the-automation-language.d: Conditions, waits and stops inside a sequence, and "the pump has been on for five minutes" is one trigger, not a timer hack.
ft.helpers.d: The values the plant's people own, like today's batch target or which shift is on: toggles, numbers, selects, text, counters, timers, and schedules. They survive restarts and they are never quietly clamped.
ft.logbook.d: State changes, writes, alarms, rule runs and config changes on one timeline, for the plant, one area, or one entity. "What happened right before?" is one list, not five screens.
ft.scripts.d: Write the clean-in-place cycle once, name it, and run it from a rule, a screen, an AI agent, or its own entity. A dry run goes through the real write gate, so you see the refusal before anything moves.
ft.recipes.d: Grade A's setpoints off the laminated sheet and into the plant in one go: checked whole, refused whole, written in order, and read back from the device. Nobody ends up with half a recipe.
ft.blueprints.d: Write a rule once with blanks and fill it in per pump. Each rule remembers the blueprint it came from, so one edit never quietly changes forty rules.
ft.dashboards.d: Build a screen by dragging cards: gauges, numbers, trends, entity lists, write buttons, script and recipe buttons, alarm lists, text, cameras, and a floor plan. Hand a dashboard to the roles that need it, or bind it to one physical screen. One layout folds from a panel PC down to a phone, so nobody ever builds the phone version. A card commands nothing itself, so a button still meets the write gate.
ft.isa-18-2-alarms.d: The industrial alarm standard, including the alarm that cleared before anyone acknowledged it, so a trip that fixed itself is still there at shift change. Shelved alarms come back in the state they are really in.
ft.notifications.d: ntfy, Gotify, Discord, webhooks, and email. Press Acknowledge on an ntfy push or in the Discord bot and the alarm is acknowledged, signed, and good for one use. The night shift answers the page from the phone in their hand.
ft.ai-agents.d: An agent can read the whole plant and touch only what you armed, through the same write gate as the screen, and never without a stated reason, which goes in the log next to the write. With writes off, nothing writes. You get an assistant that can answer "why is line 3 slow" without being able to open a valve on its own.
ft.writes-to-scaled-tags-land-right.n: Writes to scaled tags land right
ft.writes-to-scaled-tags-land-right.d: Write 55.5 to a tag scaled by 0.1 and the device gets exactly that. A value the register can't hold is refused instead of wrapping, and a recipe with a value that doesn't fit is refused whole before its first write. Check your scaled tags before you upgrade an older plant.
ft.mqtt-and-an-embedded-broker.d: Plain topics, Sparkplug B, and an optional broker in the same process, so one box can be the whole install.
ft.the-sun.d: Sunrise, sunset, dawn, dusk, and the sun's height and bearing, worked out on the box from the site's location, plus a sun trigger with an offset. A site whose uplink died three weeks ago still turns the yard lights on at dusk.
ft.mqtt-discovery.d: ESPHome, Zigbee2MQTT, Tasmota, and Shelly devices show up on their own, as read-only. Nothing is armed until a person accepts the device and arms each point, so a device announcing itself never earns the right to flip a relay.
ft.network-discovery.d: HotLoop listens for devices announcing themselves on the network and lists what each one is and how HotLoop could talk to it. Active probing stays off until you name a network, because a port sweep has knocked over PLCs. Nothing is added by itself.
ft.broker-logins-with-rules.d: A twelve dollar plug's login can't publish to the boiler's command topic. Logins carry publish and subscribe rules, checked on every message.
ft.historian-targets.d: Every reading also goes to the plant's own database: PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB, SQL Server, InfluxDB, MySQL and MariaDB. Polling never waits for a target, and one that falls behind catches up on its own.
ft.a-kafka-event-stream.d: Readings and the system log go to any Kafka-compatible broker, Apache Kafka and Redpanda included, with TLS and the standard sign-in methods. Delivery is at least once, so a reading can arrive twice after an outage. Your data team gets the plant on the bus they already run.
ft.sqlite-or-postgresql-your-pick.d: The database is a setting. A Pi runs any product on a single file with no second container. Moving between databases is a backup and a restore.
ft.updates-that-roll-themselves-back.d: Boxes that follow the stable release update themselves, and an update that can't pass its health check is rolled back instead of reported as a success. On Kubernetes you run the upgrade yourself. Either way the update that breaks at 2am goes back by itself.
ft.every-protocol-driver.d: OPC UA, CODESYS, OPC UA PubSub, Modbus, MQTT and Sparkplug B, EtherNet/IP, S7comm, MTConnect, HTTP, SNMP, BACnet/IP, and UniFi. Protocols don't split the products, so nobody runs the Gateway just to reach one PLC.
ft.codesys-by-the-names-the-programmer-g: CODESYS, by the names the programmer gave the variables

A CODESYS runtime is read and written by variable name, like Application.GVL_Line.rTemp, with nothing installed in the PLC. A download or a restart reads bad with the reason and comes back with no hands. Tested on a real runtime and on bare metal, including a program of over a hundred thousand variables read in about two seconds.
ft.opc-ua-pubsub-over-uadp.d: HotLoop listens for a publisher's data over UDP, unicast or multicast, and a lost message marks that publisher's tags uncertain until the next full update. You see a gap as a gap.
ft.unifi-network.d: Devices, ports, PoE, WAN failover, and clients as tags, and a quiet PLC tells you which switch port it is on. A backup link that has been dead for two days reads dead. Every tag is read-only until a person arms it.
ft.unifi-screens-and-events.d: An overview with the WAN strip, a topology map that zooms and pinches, switch faceplates with port traffic, clients, networks, and WiFi, one button that makes the usual alarms, and the console's event stream so a switch dropping off lands in the logbook in seconds. An agent can ask for the topology and the latest events.
ft.unifi-commands.d: A device's locate LED, a device restart, a switch port's PoE power cycle, a wireless network on or off, a client block, and a port's PoE mode, each through the write gate and each off until you arm that tag. A power cycle waits out a 15 minute cooldown, and a port that carries the network is never cycled. Proven on the lab's controller, with one power cycle of an access point on a real network.
ft.hardware-access.d: A container can share its node's network when it has to hear what the node hears, like multicast. The charts also mount the node's USB devices and Bluetooth for whatever you plug in later, which makes the container root on the node, and three switches turn that off. Zigbee comes through Zigbee2MQTT.
ft.backups-and-restore.d: One backup works in IoT, Edge, and the Gateway, and it is also how you move between them. A restore either works whole or says no.
ft.store-and-forward.d: A dead link leaves no hole in the historian upstream: Edge holds the readings and replays them in order, flagged as historical. It publishes upstream as a Sparkplug B edge node, which is the MQTT standard for industrial data. Off until you switch edge publishing on.
ft.runs-with-the-wan-dead.d: We booted a real Edge with its uplink pointed at a link that eats every packet, and the screen, a write, a script, a recipe, an automation, and an alarm all worked. A box that reboots mid-outage comes right back. Readings are held in memory first and spill to disk only when the broker stops answering, oldest replayed first, with a cap so a long outage can't fill the disk.
ft.opc-ua-server.d: The SCADA you already own sees every tag without a new driver. Read-only and secured, and Ignition reads it end to end. Off until you switch it on.
ft.opc-ua-pubsub-publisher.d: Edge can publish the tags you choose over OPC UA PubSub, full updates when values change and heartbeats when they don't. A bad tag goes out as bad, never as its last value. Off until you switch it on.
ft.panel-mode.d: A dashboard bound to a physical screen opens full bleed, with no header, no tabs, and bigger touch targets, and it works with the uplink down. Every product with a dashboard has it, not only Edge.
ft.hmi-symbols-faceplates-and-pin-sign-i: HMI symbols, faceplates and PIN sign-in
The ISA-101 symbol library, the motor and valve faceplates, and PIN sign-in for shared panels, so the audit names a person and not "panel 3". These are planned.
ft.fleet.d: Restart a relay, ask it to re-announce itself, or send it a new device file without anybody driving out to the box. Fleet knows every Edge Relay you register. Off until you switch it on, and it has no screen yet, so you drive it through the API.
ft.multi-site.d: One Gateway asks the others the questions it would answer for itself. A site that doesn't answer shows as unreachable, never as zero alarms.
ft.scheduled-reports.d: Historian numbers on a schedule, as CSV or HTML, stored and emailed. Only good readings count, and every row says how many it threw out.
nd.complete: Watches only the nodes explicitly selected in its scope, as Node-RED does.
nd.inject: Interval, startup and cron-scheduled injection are supported. The crontab is read the way Node-RED's own scheduler, cronosjs, reads it, in the process's local time, including what it does with the hour that goes missing or repeats when the clocks change. A manual inject from the admin API always sends the configured properties: Node-RED's inject-with-these-values (msg.__user_inject_props__) is not implemented.
nd.link call: Calls a Link In and sends on whatever a Link Out in return mode sends back, including calls made from inside a call. A static target is chosen by id. In dynamic mode msg.target is an id or a name, looked up on the calling flow first and then across every flow, never inside a subflow instance. A call with no return within the timeout raises an error with the original message; a return that turns up after that still goes out, as it does in Node-RED.
nd.link out: Both modes are supported: send to Link In nodes, and return to the Link Call that sent the message. One deliberate difference: a Link In that is not running, and a return with no Link Call to go back to, raise an error a Catch node can see. Node-RED drops the first quietly and only logs a warning for the second, which makes a deleted or mistyped link very hard to find.
nd.hotloop-flow-discord-bot: Flow's own Discord bot, the same bot token HotLoop core's bot uses.
nd.hotloop-flow-ethernetip: Flow's own EtherNet/IP connection, for tag access on ControlLogix, CompactLogix and Micro800 controllers. It connects on the first request, drops the connection on any failure that makes it untrustworthy, and reconnects on the next one.
nd.hotloop-flow-gotify: Flow's own Gotify server, the same settings HotLoop core publishes alarms with.
nd.hotloop-flow-hotloop: Flow's own connection to a HotLoop. Logs in with an account and sends the bearer token HotLoop hands back, and logs in again when it expires.
nd.hotloop-flow-influxdb: Flow's own InfluxDB connection, targeting the InfluxDB in the EmberNet App Store.
nd.hotloop-flow-kafka: Flow's own Kafka connection, the same settings HotLoop core's Kafka output uses.
nd.hotloop-flow-mcp-server: Flow's own connection to a Model Context Protocol server over Streamable HTTP. It sends a bearer token if it has one, connects on the first call and reconnects on the call after a failure.
nd.hotloop-flow-modbus: Flow's own Modbus TCP connection. It connects on the first request, drops the connection on any failure that makes it untrustworthy, and reconnects on the next one.
nd.hotloop-flow-ntfy: Flow's own ntfy server, the same settings HotLoop core publishes alarms with.
nd.hotloop-flow-opcua: Flow's own OPC UA connection. It connects on first use, notices when the server goes away, and opens a new session on the next request or, for a subscription, by itself with a growing wait between tries.
nd.hotloop-flow-postgres: Flow's own PostgreSQL connection. Targets the PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB apps in the EmberNet App Store.
nd.hotloop-flow-s7: Flow's own Siemens S7 connection, over ISO on TCP. It connects on the first request, drops the connection on any failure that makes it untrustworthy, and reconnects on the next one.
nd.hotloop-flow-sparkplug: Flow's own Sparkplug B connection, either as an edge node or as a host application, on MQTT 3.1.1. An edge node can wait for a primary host application's STATE before it is born and can move through a list of brokers. A host application connects to one broker. Metrics carry arrays, DataSet, Template and PropertySet values. A metric's MetaData (files and multi-part bytes) is not carried.
nd.modbus-client: TCP, RTU over TCP and serial RTU clients. It connects on the first request, drops the connection on any failure that makes it untrustworthy and reconnects on the next one, so reconnectOnTimeout and reconnectTimeout have nothing to wait for. Requests take turns on the one connection, so commandDelay, bufferCommands and the queue and state log switches have no effect. Serial ASCII (RTU-BUFFERD is accepted, ASCII is not) is not supported. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds the TCP socket to one network interface, for a box whose port carries several VLANs with the same subnet. Ignored properties: `bufferCommands`, `stateLogEnabled`, `queueLogEnabled`, `failureLogEnabled`, `commandDelay`, `reconnectOnTimeout`, `reconnectTimeout`, `parallelUnitIdsAllowed`, `serialConnectionDelay`, `serialAsciiResponseStartDelimiter`.
nd.modbustcp-server: Accepted so a flow that carries it loads and saves unchanged. The node types that read from it (modbustcp-read and modbustcp-write) are not provided, so it connects to nothing. Use modbus-client with the getter and write nodes.
nd.mqtt-broker: MQTT 3.1, 3.1.1 and 5. Connection, credentials, TLS, clean session, keepalive, and birth, close and will messages with their QoS, retain flag and, on version 5, their properties and the will delay. On version 5 also the session expiry interval and connect user properties. The receive maximum, maximum packet size and topic alias maximum settings are not implemented, and the broker's defaults apply. TLS is Node-RED's usetls with a tls-config for the CA, client certificate and server name; a broker saved by an earlier Flow with tls: true still connects over TLS with the system roots. Ignored properties: `receiveMaximum`, `maximumPacketSize`, `topicAliasMaximum`.
nd.postgreSQLConfig: A PostgreSQL or TimescaleDB connection pool on Flow's own driver. Each setting may be a string, a number, a boolean or an environment variable, by its ...FieldType companion; other types (msg, flow, global) have no message to read from in a config node and stop the node. ssl true verifies the server certificate, as node-postgres does, and ssl may also be one of disable, prefer, require, verify-full or no-verify. The password is read from the node's credential when there is one, else from the flow file's password property, as the community node keeps it. Connections open on the first query, not at deploy, and an idle connection is kept for at least a minute whatever idle says, so a plant reading once a second does not reconnect for every reading. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds the connections to one network interface, with a pool for each interface a node asks for.
nd.tls-config: Certificate, key and CA from files, from environment variables, from uploaded PEM text, or from a PKCS#12 bundle, with a passphrase for an encrypted key or bundle, server name, ALPN protocol and the verify switch. Two differences. A path is read through the secret scope, the data directory plus secrets.allowedPaths, because a TLS config that can read any path is a way to probe the filesystem from the editor. And a config that is broken, a certificate without its key or a file that is not there, fails to deploy. Node-RED logs it and carries on, so the connection quietly goes out without the client certificate you configured.
nd.ui-base: Dashboard 2 configuration, accepted so a flow that carries it loads and saves unchanged. Dashboard 2's widgets (ui-text, ui-button and the rest) are not provided, so nothing draws it. Use the ui_ nodes.
nd.ui-group: Dashboard 2 configuration, accepted so a flow that carries it loads and saves unchanged. Dashboard 2's widgets (ui-text, ui-button and the rest) are not provided, so nothing draws it. Use the ui_ nodes.
nd.ui-page: Dashboard 2 configuration, accepted so a flow that carries it loads and saves unchanged. Dashboard 2's widgets (ui-text, ui-button and the rest) are not provided, so nothing draws it. Use the ui_ nodes.
nd.ui-theme: Dashboard 2 configuration, accepted so a flow that carries it loads and saves unchanged. Dashboard 2's widgets (ui-text, ui-button and the rest) are not provided, so nothing draws it. Use the ui_ nodes.
nd.ui_base: The dashboard's theme: its name (dark or light) and base color are used. Custom fonts, sizes, widget colors and the site title are accepted and not applied.
nd.ui_group: A card on a tab, width columns wide, in the tab's order. Its widgets are laid out in a grid of that many columns.
nd.ui_link: A menu entry that opens another address, http or https only. The icon is accepted and not drawn.
nd.ui_spacer: An empty cell in the group's grid, width columns by height rows. It shows nothing and sends nothing.
nd.ui_tab: A page of the dashboard, in the menu by its order. The icon is accepted and not drawn. A disabled or hidden tab is left out.
nd.websocket-client: Connects out and reconnects on its own when the connection drops, in payload mode or whole-message mode. A wss:// URL checks the server against the system roots, or against a tls-config's CA, with its client certificate and server name, as in Node-RED.
nd.websocket-listener: Serves a websocket path, in payload mode or whole-message mode. The path shares the flow route table with the HTTP In nodes, so it cannot shadow the editor or the admin API and cannot collide with another node's path. A client that stops reading is disconnected rather than queued without limit, which Node-RED does not do.
nd.netinfo: Flow's own node. Reports the interfaces the runtime can see, which in macvlan mode is how a flow learns its address on the OT VLAN.
nd.scan: Flow's own node. Sweeps a CIDR range for OT devices and identifies Modbus and EtherNet/IP endpoints. Bounded by the discovery allowlist in the runtime configuration, not by this dialog.
nd.change: set, change, delete and move are supported for msg, flow and global targets, including JSONata-typed values. The deep copy option is ignored: a value set from another property is shared with it, as it is in Node-RED with the option off. Ignored properties: `dc`.
nd.delay: All six modes are implemented, fixed, variable, random, rate limit, per-topic queue and timed release, along with msg.reset, msg.flush and the second output for dropped messages. Two deliberate differences: the queue is bounded, and past the limit a message is refused to a Catch node rather than held, because Node-RED's unbounded queue turns a source faster than the drain into an OOM-kill with no explanation; and messages still held when the flow stops are released rather than discarded.
nd.exec: The three outputs, both buffered and streaming modes, the timeout and the appended message property all behave as Node-RED's do. Two things do not, and neither is negotiable. There is no shell: the command line is split on quoting rules only, and an unquoted shell metacharacter is refused rather than run, so one allowed command cannot become an arbitrary one. And the node is disabled until an operator names the commands a flow may run. Node-RED's exec node runs anything, and Node-RED starts with no authentication by default; a vendor shipping that default became CVE-2025-41656 (Pilz IndustrialPI 4, VDE-2025-045), unauthenticated command execution on the device. Output is capped per stream; a command that exceeds it is killed and reported rather than being allowed to fill the heap. A command that forks children of its own may leave them behind when it is killed.
nd.function: Runs on the JavaScript interpreter, a JavaScript interpreter written in Go, rather than Node's vm module. The language is ES2023; the Node standard library is not present. require() and npm modules do not work and cannot be made to without embedding Node. There is always a CPU time limit, which Node-RED leaves optional and off, and it applies to every timer callback too. setTimeout, setInterval and their clear functions work, on the node's clock, and every one is cleared when the flow stops or is redeployed. Buffer is there (alloc, from, concat, the read and write methods for integers and floats in both byte orders, slice, toString and toJSON). A byte slice in a message arrives as a byte array, so wrap it with Buffer.from. Ignored properties: `libs`, `require`.
nd.rbe: Block-unless-changed and deadband modes are supported. Narrowband modes are not implemented in this build.
nd.switch: Every comparison rule is supported, including a JSONata expression rule, which sees $I and $N for a message that is part of a sequence. The sequence rules head, tail and index are not implemented, and a rule using one fails every message with an unknown operator error. Ignored properties: `head`, `tail`, `index`.
nd.template: Mustache templating is implemented against mustache.js's dialect, including its HTML escape set and standalone-line handling, so a template moved from Node-RED renders the same bytes. Partials ({{>name}}) and custom delimiters are refused rather than ignored, because there is nothing in a flow file that can supply either.
nd.trigger: Both messages, extend-on-retrigger, wait-to-be-reset, msg.reset, the msg.delay override, per-topic grouping and the second output are implemented. The divergence is the same as the Delay node's: the number of simultaneously armed timers is bounded, and a message past the limit is refused to a Catch node rather than silently arming another. Timers with a deadline that are still armed when the flow stops fire immediately rather than being discarded; a timer waiting to be reset is dropped, because firing it would invent an event that never happened.
nd.ui_button: A press sends the payload and topic, each by its type (a literal, a flow or global value, a property of the last message, the time). The icon is accepted and not drawn. Ignored properties: `icon`.
nd.ui_chart: Line and bar charts of numbers over time, one line for each msg.topic, kept for removeOlder times its unit and at most removeOlderPoints points a line. A payload of [] clears it. Pie, polar, radar and horizontal bar are drawn as a line. Charts built from an array of series objects, and the output on a click of a point, are not provided. Ignored properties: `cutout`, `useDifferentColor`, `outputs`.
nd.ui_gauge: Gauge, donut, compass and wave, drawn on a canvas, in the three sector colors. The difference mode of the donut is accepted and drawn as the plain donut.
nd.ui_led: Draws a light whose color is the first entry of colorForValue that equals msg.payload, as a boolean, a number or text, or msg.color when allowed.
nd.ui_numeric: A message with a numeric payload sets the value, and with passthru on it goes on unchanged. The operator's change sends {payload, topic}, within min and max. wrap is accepted and ignored: the value stops at the limits.
nd.ui_switch: A click sends the on or the off value. With decouple off the switch moves at once, and with it on it moves only when a message with the value arrives. A message whose payload equals the on or the off value sets the switch. The icons and animate are accepted and not drawn. Ignored properties: `onicon`, `officon`, `animate`.
nd.ui_template: HTML with a small AngularJS-style layer: {{ }}, ng-click, ng-class, ng-init, ng-show, ng-hide, ng-if, ng-bind, scope.msg, scope.$watch, scope.send and scope.$eval. Directives beyond those (ng-repeat, ng-model, ng-switch, controllers, Angular Material components) are not provided. The template runs in the operator's browser with the page's own permissions, so it is as trusted as the flow's author. Global scope is treated as local.
nd.ui_text:
Shows msg.payload through the value format, with {{msg.x}} and {{value}} and the number filter ({{msg.payload \| number:1}}). The label may contain
, and no other markup. Angular's other filters are not supported.
nd.ui_text_input: Sends the text, or the number in number mode, after delay milliseconds without typing, on Enter, or on leaving the box when sendOnBlur is on. A message sets the text.
nd.e-mail: Sends msg.payload as the body and msg.topic as the subject, to the node's To (the name property) or, when that is empty, msg.to. msg.cc, msg.bcc, msg.from, msg.html and msg.attachments ([{filename, content, contentType}]) are honored, and a Buffer payload goes as an attachment. secure is an encrypted connection from the first byte (port 465). Otherwise the node asks for STARTTLS when the server offers it. tls means only connect to a server with a valid certificate. Authentication is BASIC (PLAIN, or LOGIN as a fallback), XOAUTH2 with the access token read from the message property in token, or NONE. A password is refused over a connection that is not encrypted unless the server is this host. Sending only: the e-mail in node (reading a mailbox) is not provided. msg.header and the saslformat switch are ignored. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) sends the connection over one network interface. Ignored properties: `saslformat`.
nd.ethernetip read: Flow's own EtherNet/IP tag read. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-cip-ethernet-ip, which does not run here.
nd.ethernetip write: Flow's own EtherNet/IP tag write. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-cip-ethernet-ip, which does not run here.
nd.hotloop in: Flow's own node. It follows HotLoop's live feed, which has no Node-RED counterpart.
nd.hotloop recipe: Flow's own node. It applies a HotLoop recipe.
nd.hotloop script: Flow's own node. It runs a HotLoop script.
nd.hotloop state: Flow's own node. It reads one entity's state from HotLoop.
nd.http in: Serves a path, with Express-style :params and a trailing *, and builds the same msg.req / msg.res / msg.payload shape Node-RED does, including JSON, form-encoded and raw bodies. Three deliberate differences. A request that no HTTP Response node answers is closed with 504 after a timeout instead of being held open forever, because Node-RED's version leaks a connection per request until the process runs out of sockets and stops answering with nothing in the log. Two nodes claiming the same method and path is refused at deploy time rather than one of them silently never firing. And a path that would shadow the editor or the admin API is refused for the same reason. Uploads parse the way multer does in Node-RED: text fields into msg.payload, files into msg.req.files, a broken upload answered with 500. One bound multer lacks: an array index over 10,000 in a field name, a[99999999], is refused instead of building a sparse array that long. msg.req.cookies is cookie-parser's, j: values included. Ignored properties: `swaggerDoc`.
nd.http request: Method, URL, headers, basic authentication, redirects and the three return types, with msg.url, msg.method and msg.headers overriding the node. The response body is size-capped and the call is bounded by a timeout, neither of which Node-RED does. TLS comes from a tls-config, or without one msg.rejectUnauthorized = false skips the certificate check for that one message, as in Node-RED. msg.cookies and a cookie header go out through a cookie jar, cookies a redirect sets follow the redirect, and msg.responseCookies and msg.redirectList come back, all as in Node-RED. A multipart/form-data content type with an object payload sends it as a form. Proxy settings and connection persistence are not implemented in this build. There is no egress allowlist: this node can reach anything the pod can, exactly as Node-RED's can, and the place to bound that is a NetworkPolicy rather than an edit dialog nobody outside the cluster can trust. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds the connections to one network interface. Ignored properties: `proxy`, `persist`.
nd.http response: Status code and headers from the node or from msg.statusCode and msg.headers, with the payload as the body. msg.cookies sets and clears cookies exactly as Express does for Node-RED, options and all; with more than one, they go out in name order rather than the order the object was built in.
nd.mcp client: Flow's own node. It calls a tool on a Model Context Protocol server, or lists the tools it has.
nd.mcp result: Flow's own node. It answers the call an mcp tool node started.
nd.mcp tool: Flow's own node. It serves a flow as an agent tool, for a caller authenticated like the admin API's, and it has no Node-RED counterpart.
nd.modbus read: Flow's own Modbus TCP read. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-modbus, which does not run here.
nd.modbus write: Flow's own Modbus TCP write. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-modbus, which does not run here.
nd.modbus-flex-getter: Takes {fc, unitid, address, quantity} from msg.payload. Output and failures as the Getter. The I/O file (useIOFile) is not supported, and a node that asks for one does not start. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds this node's connection to one network interface. Without it the node's tab's FLOW_NETWORK_INTERFACE, then the client's interface, then the host's choice. Ignored properties: `useIOFile`, `ioFile`, `useIOForPayload`, `logIOActivities`.
nd.modbus-flex-write: Takes {value, fc, unitid, address, quantity} from msg.payload. Output and failures as the Write node. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds this node's connection to one network interface. Without it the node's tab's FLOW_NETWORK_INTERFACE, then the client's interface, then the host's choice.
nd.modbus-getter: Reads on a message, from the node's own address and quantity. The output carries msg.payload, msg.responseBuffer ({data, buffer}), msg.input and msg.modbusRequest. A failure goes out the second output with msg.error, and out the first as an empty message when emptyMsgOnFail is set. The I/O file (useIOFile) is not supported, and a node that asks for one does not start. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds this node's connection to one network interface. Without it the node's tab's FLOW_NETWORK_INTERFACE, then the client's interface, then the host's choice. Ignored properties: `useIOFile`, `ioFile`, `useIOForPayload`, `logIOActivities`.
nd.modbus-read: Polls every rate rateUnit once the flow starts (after startDelayTime when delayOnStart is set), and reads when a message arrives. Output as the Getter, with msg.topic set from the node. The I/O file (useIOFile) is not supported, and a node that asks for one does not start. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds this node's connection to one network interface. Without it the node's tab's FLOW_NETWORK_INTERFACE, then the client's interface, then the host's choice. Ignored properties: `useIOFile`, `ioFile`, `useIOForPayload`, `logIOActivities`.
nd.modbus-server: A Modbus TCP server over four buffers (coils, holding registers, input registers, discrete inputs) of the sizes the node sets. A message with msg.payload = {register, address, value} sets values, where register is holding, coils, input or discrete and value is one value or a list. A client's write comes out the first output (holding registers) or the second (coils). The third and fourth outputs belong to input registers and discrete inputs, which a client cannot write, so they send nothing, and the fifth carries errors. Requests on every unit id are answered from the same buffers. Serial is not supported. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds the listening socket to one network interface before it listens, so a box with a VLAN for each machine can run one server on each VLAN at the same address and port. The node's own setting wins, then the tab's FLOW_NETWORK_INTERFACE. Ignored properties: `logEnabled`, `showStatusActivities`.
nd.modbus-write: Writes msg.payload (a value, or a list the length of quantity) with function code 5, 6, 15 or 16, whichever fits. The output is the incoming message with msg.responseBuffer, and failures go out the second output. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds this node's connection to one network interface. Without it the node's tab's FLOW_NETWORK_INTERFACE, then the client's interface, then the host's choice. Ignored properties: `logIOActivities`.
nd.mqtt in: Topic subscription with QoS and payload decoding, and on MQTT 5 the no local, retain as published and retain handling options, with the message's properties on msg.userProperties, msg.contentType, msg.responseTopic, msg.correlationData and msg.messageExpiryInterval, and its content type steering the auto-detect decoding the way Node-RED's does. Dynamic subscription via a control message is not implemented.
nd.mqtt out: Publishing with topic, QoS and retain from the node or the message, and on MQTT 5 the content type, response topic, correlation data, message expiry and user properties, from the node or from msg.contentType, msg.responseTopic, msg.correlationData, msg.messageExpiryInterval and msg.userProperties, with msg.responseTopic as the topic when there is no other. Topic aliases are not used: the full topic always goes. The connect and disconnect control messages are not implemented. Ignored properties: `topicAlias`.
nd.opcua read: Flow's own OPC UA read. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-opcua, which does not run here.
nd.opcua subscribe: Flow's own OPC UA subscription. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-opcua, which does not run here.
nd.opcua write: Flow's own OPC UA write. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-opcua, which does not run here.
nd.s7 read: Flow's own Siemens S7 read. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-s7, which does not run here.
nd.s7 write: Flow's own Siemens S7 write. Not the same configuration as the community node-red-contrib-s7, which does not run here.
nd.sparkplug command: Flow's own Sparkplug B command sender, as a host application.
nd.sparkplug in: Flow's own Sparkplug B listener. On a host connection it follows every edge node it can see. On an edge connection it hands over the commands sent to it.
nd.sparkplug out: Flow's own Sparkplug B publisher, for an edge node or one of its devices.
nd.tcp in: Listens or connects out, in stream mode with a delimiter or single mode collecting until the peer closes, with buffer, string or base64 payloads. Every message carries msg._session so a TCP Out node can reply on the same connection. Three bounds Node-RED does not have: the number of accepted connections, the size of one delimited message, and the total of a single-mode read. A peer that opens connections and never closes them, or sends without ever sending the delimiter, grows the heap until the pod dies otherwise. TLS through a tls-config works both ways: a listener presents the config's certificate, a client checks the server's.
nd.tcp out: Connects to a host and sends, or replies on the connection a TCP In node accepted, found through msg._session. Listening for inbound connections purely to write to them, which Node-RED's third mode does, is not implemented, use a TCP In node for the listening half and this node in reply mode. TLS through a tls-config applies to client mode; a reply goes back down whatever the TCP In node accepted, TLS or not.
nd.tcp request: Connects, sends the payload and waits for the reply, in any of Node-RED's four wait modes: a fixed time, a delimiter, a byte count, or until the peer closes. msg.host and msg.port override the node. Every request opens its own connection, Node-RED's connection-reuse mode is not implemented, and reusing one would change the semantics of the wait modes, which all end at a connection boundary. With a tls-config the server's certificate is checked unless the config says not to. Node-RED's TCP Request never checks it, whatever the config says, which makes its TLS a padlock painted on the door. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds the connection to one network interface.
nd.udp in: Receives datagrams, optionally joining a multicast group, with buffer, string or base64 payloads and the sender's address on msg.ip and msg.port. IPv6 and per-node interface selection are not implemented in this build. Ignored properties: `ipv6`.
nd.udp out: Sends datagrams to a host, a broadcast address or a multicast group, with msg.ip and msg.port overriding the node. IPv6 is not implemented in this build. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds the socket to one network interface. Ignored properties: `ipv6`.
nd.websocket in: Emits a message per frame, carrying msg._session so a WebSocket Out node can reply to the connection it came from.
nd.websocket out: Replies to the connection named by msg._session, or broadcasts to every open connection when there is none, as Node-RED does. The divergence is what happens when a connection cannot keep up: the frame is refused to a Catch node and the connection is closed, rather than queued without limit. Blocking instead would push back-pressure from a slow browser into the flow's scheduler, which is a worse failure than losing a connection that had already stopped reading.
nd.csv: Parsing to objects and rendering from objects are supported, with configurable separator and header handling. Multi-line quoted fields spanning separate messages are not reassembled.
nd.html: Extracts elements by CSS selector, returning inner HTML, text or attributes, as one message per match or one message holding an array. The selector engine covers type, id, class, attribute, descendant, child and comma groups. Pseudo-classes, pseudo-elements, sibling combinators and the ~= and \|= attribute operators are refused at deploy time rather than ignored, because a selector that quietly drops its :nth-child matches the wrong elements and keeps working. Returned HTML is re-rendered from the parse tree, so it is normalized markup rather than the original bytes.
nd.json: Conversion in both directions is supported. Schema validation is supported, against msg.schema as in Node-RED and against a schema in the node's settings. The validator is not Ajv: it reads draft 2020-12 unless the schema names another draft, it refuses a $ref to anything outside the schema, and format keywords it does not know are ignored.
nd.xml: Both directions, using xml2js's object convention: attributes under the key named by "attr" (default $), element text under "chr" (default _), and every child element as an array, which is xml2js's own explicitArray default. Set ew_explicitArray to false to collapse single children instead. The per-message msg.options that Node-RED passes through to xml2js is not honored, the other xml2js options change the shape of the output, and silently ignoring one would produce an object the flow does not expect while looking like it worked. Namespaces are kept as part of the element name rather than being resolved. Ignored properties: `options`.
nd.yaml: Conversion in both directions, toggling on the value's type when no action is set, as Node-RED's does.
nd.batch: Group by count with overlap and with the end of an incoming sequence honored, group by time interval with or without empty sequences, and concatenate sequences by topic, with msg.reset, as Node-RED does. Two configurations Node-RED accepts are refused: a count below one, which it quietly reads as one, and an interval of zero, which holds every message forever.
nd.join: Automatic, manual and reduce modes as Node-RED has them: placement by msg.parts.index, the separator Split recorded, nested sequences, arrays, strings, buffers, objects keyed by a message property, merged objects, accumulate, msg.complete, msg.reset, msg.restartTimeout, the timeout, and a reduce expression with $A, $I and $N and an optional fixup. One deliberate difference: an automatic join given a message without msg.parts raises an error rather than logging a warning.
nd.sort: Sorts an array property by its elements or by a JSONata key evaluated against each element, and a message sequence by a property or a JSONata key evaluated against each message.
nd.split: Splits arrays, objects, strings and buffers, by delimiter, by a byte sequence or by length, including streaming mode, which carries an unfinished piece over to the next message. msg.parts matches Node-RED's, separator and nested sequences included. Three deliberate differences: an object is split in sorted key order, because Go maps have none; a string is split by length in characters rather than UTF-16 code units, so no character is cut in half; and a payload that cannot be split raises an error instead of vanishing.
nd.file: Append, overwrite and delete, with the filename from a literal, a message property, context or the environment, and utf8, base64, hex or raw encodings. The divergence is the path scope: the file nodes may only reach the data directory and whatever else the operator listed, resolved through symlinks so a link planted on the PVC cannot point out of it. Node-RED's file nodes take any path, which makes editing a flow equivalent to reading any file the process can. Writes are fsynced by default, which Node-RED's are not.
nd.file in: Whole-file, per-line and chunked reads, with utf8, base64, hex or raw output. Same path scope as the File node, and for the same reason. A read is also size-capped: Node-RED reads a whole file into memory with no limit, so pointing the node at the wrong path is an OOM-kill rather than an error. Past the cap the node says which limit was hit and that per-line or chunked mode would work.
nd.influxdb out: Flow's own node. The type name matches the community node-red-contrib-influxdb so an imported flow finds it, but the configuration is not identical, check the fields after importing.
nd.postgres: Flow's own node. Writes to and reads from PostgreSQL or TimescaleDB, with batch insert for message sequences.
nd.postgresql: Runs the query as a Mustache template against the message ({{{msg.topic}}} and {{{topic}}} both work, and put a value in as text, so prefer $1, $2 with msg.params, which go to the database as parameters). msg.payload is the list of rows and msg.pgsql is {command, rowCount}. With split on, the rows go out rowsPerMsg at a time (a row object when it is 1, else a list) with msg.parts, and a second output, when there are two, sends one message when the last group is out. msg.queryParameters (named parameters) is not supported. A failed query raises an error for a Catch node. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) sends this node's queries over one network interface.
nd.watch: Reports files and directories appearing, changing and being removed, with the same message shape Node-RED produces. It polls rather than using the kernel's notification interface, so a change is seen within the poll interval rather than immediately, and two changes inside one interval are reported once. That is a deliberate trade: fsnotify means per-platform code and a filename suffix that is a build constraint, which has already cost this codebase a day. Same path scope as the other file nodes, and the number of watched entries is capped so a recursive watch on a large tree cannot stall the runtime.
